findings.title: 2D views have no orientation letters, slice index, or coordinate annotation — with a global radiological toggle this is a laterality hazard
findings.claim: The overlay pass enumerates "crosshair, cut-plane gizmo, contours on slices, annotations, orientation cube, scale bar" — there are no L/R/A/P/S/I letters on the edges of the 2D views, no slice index/coordinate burned into the corner, and no visual indication of which display convention is active. §3 defines a global `radiological` toggle that silently mirrors left and right. A user who flips that toggle (or opens a scene saved by someone who did) has no on-screen way to tell, and every screenshot they export is ambiguous about laterality. Freeview puts orientation letters on every 2D pane and exposes a first-class toolbar toggle for coordinate annotation; NiiVue draws orientation labels by default. This is the one class of viewer bug that produces wrong-hemisphere conclusions in a paper.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:231 lists the entire overlay pass with no orientation labels; grep for "orientation" across docs/ returns only "orientation cube" (3D, ROADMAP Phase 3) and "fixed orientation" (§7.5 cameras). §3 line 65: "Default display convention is neurological (subject left on screen left) with a global radiological toggle." Freeview's toolbar exposes "coordinate annotation" and "color scale display" as top-level buttons (surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/fswiki/FreeviewGuide/FreeviewGeneralUsage/FreeviewInterface).
findings.fix: Add to §7.2 overlay pass, Phase 1 (not Phase 3): per-2D-view edge labels driven by the world axes and the radiological flag (`L`/`R`/`A`/`P`/`S`/`I`, always derived from the affine, never hardcoded per pane); a corner annotation block showing view name, slice index of the active volume layer, and world RAS of the current slice plane; a persistent `RAD`/`NEU` badge whenever `radiological === true`. Add `annotations: { orientationLabels: boolean; cornerInfo: boolean; convention badge always-on }` to `Scene`, and make orientation labels part of every Playwright golden screenshot so a regression that drops them fails CI. Add a real-data screenshot test asserting the letter at the left edge of the axial pane flips when `radiological` is toggled.

findings.title: Surface parcellations (.annot / .label.gii) can be parsed but cannot be displayed — MeshLayer has no label colour mode
findings.claim: §6.2 declares `read_fs_annot(bytes) -> Result<(Field /*label ids*/, LabelTable)>`, but `LabelTable` is never defined in §6's common types, and `MeshLayer.colorMode` is only `'tag'|'field'|'solid'`. There is no way to bind a per-node integer label field plus its colour table to a surface, no per-region visibility, and no region outlines on a surface — the exact thing the user asked for ("import regions and atlases in colors and outlines"). The same gap hits `.label.gii`, which §6.2 says lands as "node Field(s)" with the label table dropped on the floor. The test data ships six annots that would be unviewable.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:176 (`read_fs_annot`), :107 (`colorMode:'tag'|'field'|'solid'`), :173 (label.gii → "node Field(s)"). No `LabelTable` in §6 common types (:148-154). Real annots present: /Users/idohaber/datasets/000/derivatives/SimNIBS/sub-ernie/m2m_ernie/segmentation/{lh,rh}.ernie_DK40.annot, .ernie_a2009s.annot, .ernie_HCP_MMP1.annot. AGENTS.md:14 lists lh.ernie_DK40.annot as required test data, so the roadmap already assumes it loads.
findings.fix: Define `LabelTable { entries: { id: u32, name: String, color: [u8;4] }[] }` in §6 common types and reuse it for both volume LUTs and surface annots (one type, one parser family). Add `colorMode:'label'` to `MeshLayer` with `label?: { source:'node', name: string, table: LabelTable, mode:'fill'|'outline'|'both', outlineWidthPx: number, visibleLabels?: Uint32Array, perLabelOpacity?: Record<number, number> }`. §7.4: region outlines on a surface are drawn by comparing the flat label id across triangle edges in the fragment shader (de-indexed geometry, `flat in uint label`) — same trick as §7.3's screen-space label outline. Land in Phase 2 alongside the mesh layer, with a screenshot test on lh.ernie_DK40.annot over lh.central.gii.

findings.title: No per-tissue opacity or per-tissue colour override — the user's explicit "transparency of skin/skull" is not expressible
findings.claim: `MeshLayer` has a single scalar `opacity` and `tagVisibility: Record<tag, boolean>` (binary on/off). The single most common head-model view — semi-transparent scalp and skull over an opaque, field-coloured grey matter — cannot be built: you can only hide scalp entirely or make the whole mesh translucent including GM. Tag colours live on the immutable `MeshDataset` (`tags[].color`), so the user cannot recolour a tissue either. Gmsh does both (per-physical-group colour and per-view transparency); this is the headline picture in every TI/tDCS paper. It also has a rendering consequence the contract has not accounted for: §7.2's transparent pass sorts "by layer order then back-to-front per object", but with per-tag alpha a single mesh layer contributes several differently-transparent shells that must be sorted against each other and against opaque geometry.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:105-110: `MeshLayer { ... opacity; ... tagVisibility: Record<tag, boolean>; ... }`; :92 puts `color` on the dataset, which :76 declares "immutable after load". User requirement verbatim: "transparency of skin/skull". SimNIBS's own Gmsh sidecar sets per-tag colours (Mesh.Color.One..Nineteen) and per-tag visibility (`Hide "*"; Show { Volume{1002,1006}; ... }`) in /Users/idohaber/datasets/000/derivatives/SimNIBS/sub-ernie/m2m_ernie/ernie.msh.opt.
findings.fix: Replace `tagVisibility` with `tagStyle: Record<number, { visible: boolean; opacity: number; color?: vec4 }>` on `MeshLayer`, defaulting from the dataset tag table. In §7.2, state that `tag_surfaces` produces one draw per tag so per-tag alpha sorts naturally: opaque tags go in pass 1, tags with `opacity < 1` are appended to the transparent list and sorted back-to-front by tag-centroid depth. In §8, the mesh property editor is a tissue table (name from `$PhysicalNames`, colour swatch, eye, opacity slider) — not a list of checkboxes. Phase 2, with a golden screenshot of ernie showing scalp @0.2 / skull @0.35 / GM opaque.

findings.title: No load progress or cancellation anywhere in the worker protocol — a 400-500 MB mesh will look like a hang
findings.claim: §6.4's worker API is request→result only; §5 says requests carry ids and use latest-wins, with no progress channel and no cancel op. Electron main reads the whole file and gunzips it before handing over an ArrayBuffer, so nothing can report progress during the read either. The perf table budgets 4 s for ernie.msh (176 MB) — but the test tree contains meshes up to 496 MB, and the everyday TI output is a 255 MB `_TI.msh`. Four to fifteen seconds of a frozen window with no spinner, no byte counter, no cancel button is exactly the "laggy" feeling the requirement forbids, and it is the difference between feeling faster than Gmsh and feeling broken. There is also no way to abandon a mis-clicked 500 MB load.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:136-138 (latest-wins, no progress), :206-216 (§6.4 API: no progress/cancel), :141-142 (main gunzips whole file before sending), :287 (budget stated only for ernie.msh). Actual file sizes measured: m2m_ernie/ernie_seeg.msh 492,090,201 B; flex_.../TI/mesh/..._TI.msh 396,601,700 B; Simulations/docs_example/TI/mesh/docs_example_TI.msh 255,005,467 B; m2m_ernie-seeg/ernie-seeg.msh 496,603,805 B.
findings.fix: Extend the worker protocol in §6.4 with `{ type:'progress', requestId, phase:'read'|'inflate'|'parse'|'topology'|'upload', done: number, total: number }` messages, and a `cancel(requestId)` that the Rust side polls via a shared `AbortFlag` at section boundaries (per 1 M nodes/elements). Make Electron main stream the file in chunks and emit read progress. Add to §8: a per-dataset load card in the layer panel showing phase + percent + elapsed, a Cancel button, and a "first frame in N ms" line in the status bar. Add a Phase-1 gate: opening `ernie_seeg.msh` (492 MB) shows a moving progress bar within 200 ms and cancels within 500 ms of the click. Also add a §9 row for a 500 MB mesh, and state the wasm32 4 GB linear-memory ceiling plus the fact that WASM memory never shrinks — so `free(handle)` must be paired with a worker-recycle policy, or a session that opens three 400 MB meshes in sequence will OOM the tab.

findings.title: Stat-map colour mapping cannot express FreeSurfer/Freeview heatscale (min/mid/max) or a separate negative branch
findings.claim: The display model is `window:[lo,hi]` + `threshold:{lo,hi,symmetric,mode}` + a single `colormap`. That is a linear two-point ramp. The overwhelmingly dominant convention for functional/statistical overlays in this community is the three-point heatscale (min = threshold below which nothing is drawn, mid = orange, max = saturating yellow) with independent `Truncate` (hide negatives) and `Inverse` (flip sign) switches, and a mirrored blue-cyan ramp for the negative tail. `symmetric: boolean` + a `bwr` diverging map gives a linear ramp through white at zero, which is not the same picture and cannot reproduce a figure a reviewer has seen before. Users will export a map that looks nothing like the one in their paper.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:102-104 and :264-266. Freeview's documented `heatscale=min,mid,max` parameter (e.g. `freeview -v sig.nii:colormap=heat:heatscale=2,2,4`) and the overlay configuration's Truncate ("turn off the display of negative values") and Inverse ("reverse the sign of the values as they are drawn in the color scale") checkboxes — surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/fswiki/FsTutorial/MultiModalFmriIndividual_freeview and the TkSurferOverlay page. The same three-point convention is what `freesurfer-heat` in §7.6 is named after, yet the layer model has nowhere to put `mid`.
findings.fix: Change the scalar display model in §4 to `scale: { kind:'linear', lo, hi } | { kind:'heat', min, mid, max, truncate: boolean, inverse: boolean, negative: 'mirror'|'hide'|'separate' }` and give `VolumeLayer`, `MeshLayer` (field mode) and `IsosurfaceLayer` the same field so surfaces and volumes behave identically. §7.3/§7.6: build the 256×1 LUT on the CPU from the scale spec (the shader stays a single texture fetch, so heat costs nothing extra); when `negative:'separate'`, bake a 512×1 signed LUT with the dead band around zero. Add `colormapNegative` to §7.6's list (blue→cyan default). Phase 2, gated by a screenshot of a subject_TI_max overlay at heatscale 0.05/0.1/0.2.

findings.title: Colour bars are Phase 3 — every screenshot taken before then is scientifically unusable
findings.claim: "colour bars" appear only in ROADMAP Phase 3, next to the orientation cube and measurement tool. But §8 ships Screenshot in Phase 2, and Phase 2's own gate is "every feature has a screenshot test". A field or stat map rendered without a colour bar has no units and no range — it is a picture, not a result. Freeview puts colour-scale display on the main toolbar; NiiVue enables it with `isColorbar: true`; Gmsh turns it on by default (SimNIBS's shipped sidecar sets `View[0].ShowScale = 1`). Shipping thresholding, windowing, and screenshots one whole phase before the legend that explains them inverts the dependency.
findings.evidence: ROADMAP.md:26 (Phase 3: "...scale bar, colour bars, measurement tool") vs ROADMAP.md:22 (Phase 2: "screenshot 1×/2×/4×"). ARCHITECTURE.md:231 omits colour bars from the overlay pass entirely. `View[0].ShowScale = 1;` in /Users/idohaber/datasets/000/derivatives/SimNIBS/sub-ernie/Simulations/docs_example/TI/mesh/docs_example_TI.msh.opt. NiiVue `isColorbar` / `colorbarVisible` per-volume (niivue.com/docs/options).
findings.fix: Move colour bars into Phase 2 and add them to §7.2's overlay pass: one bar per visible scalar layer, showing colormap, numeric ticks at the scale endpoints (and `mid` for heat), the threshold cut as a notch, the field name, and a units string (`Field.units`, read from NIfTI `xyz_units`/`intent_name` and from the Gmsh view name — add a `units?: string` to `Field`). Per-layer `showColorbar: boolean`, position configurable (right/bottom), and required to be included in screenshots. Same phase move for the scale bar on 2D views.

findings.title: No active-layer concept; window/level is bound to "the top volume layer"
findings.claim: §7.5 says right-drag does window/level "on the top volume layer". In the normal stack — T1 at the bottom, TI_max overlay above it, an atlas on top — the topmost volume layer is the atlas, which is a label map that has no meaningful window. The user's intent is always "the layer I have selected in the panel", which is how Freeview works (the layer list has an active/highlighted row, and edits apply to it). `Scene` has no `activeLayerId`, so every layer-directed interaction (window/level drag, threshold keys, opacity keys, delete, reorder) has no defined target, and the UI panel selection has no engine-side counterpart — which contradicts §8's rule that everything must be reachable from the engine API alone.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:258-259 ("right-drag = window/level on the top volume layer"), :115 (`Scene = { datasets, layers, views, cursor, radiological, background, lighting }` — no active layer), :279 ("Everything the UI can do must be reachable from `engine` API alone"). Freeview: "Volumes can be toggled visible/active via checkboxes and are highlighted when selected for editing operations" (FreeviewInterface).
findings.fix: Add `activeLayerId: LayerId | null` to `Scene` and `engine.setActiveLayer(id)`. Rebind §7.5: right-drag = window/level on the **active** layer (falling back to the topmost non-label volume layer if the active layer has no window); add keys `[`/`]` cycle active layer, `v` toggle its visibility, `Shift+drag` its opacity, `Ctrl+↑/↓` reorder it. Draw a 1 px accent border on the active layer's row and, per Freeview, a coloured border on the active view pane. Phase 1 (it is part of the layer/scene store, not a feature).

findings.title: `.msh.opt` sidecars are ignored, so every SimNIBS mesh opens looking worse than it does in Gmsh
findings.claim: SimNIBS writes a `<mesh>.msh.opt` next to every mesh it produces. It carries the tissue names, the per-tissue RGB palette, the default visibility set, the field's default colour range, the colormap choice, and whether the scale bar is shown. Nothing in the contract reads it. Consequence: double-click a `_TI.msh` and Tetravox shows an opaque scalp shell with a full-data-range colormap, while Gmsh shows exactly grey matter and eyeballs, TI_max windowed to [0, 0.1222], colour bar on. The first ten seconds with the product are a side-by-side loss against the tool it is meant to replace — and the fix is a 150-line parser for a handful of keys.
findings.evidence: Measured. /Users/idohaber/datasets/000/derivatives/SimNIBS/sub-ernie/Simulations/docs_example/TI/mesh/docs_example_TI.msh.opt contains `View[0].CustomMin = 0.0; View[0].CustomMax = 0.12217871837158231; View[0].RangeType = 2; View[0].SaturateValues = 1; View[0].ColormapNumber = 2; View[0].ShowScale = 1;` and `Hide "*"; Show { Volume{1002,1006}; Surface{1002,1006}; ... }`. /Users/idohaber/.../m2m_ernie/ernie.msh.opt adds `Physical Volume (" WM",1) = { 1 };` … `Physical Surface (" Internal_air_surface",1099)` and `Mesh.Color.One = {230,230,230}; … Mesh.Color.Nineteen = {221,141,135};`. A `.msh.opt` sits beside every one of the 8+ large meshes in the tree. ARCHITECTURE.md §6.2 (:171-186) never mentions it.
findings.fix: Add to §6.2: `pub fn read_msh_opt(bytes:&[u8]) -> Result<MshOptions>` parsing only `Physical Volume/Surface ("name",tag)`, `Mesh.Color.<Ordinal>`, `Hide`/`Show { Volume{…}; Surface{…}; }`, and `View[N].{CustomMin,CustomMax,RangeType,SaturateValues,ColormapNumber,ShowScale,VectorType}`. §8: when opening `X.msh`, auto-load `X.msh.opt` if present and use it to seed the initial `MeshLayer` (tag colours, tagStyle visibility, field scale, colorbar on); show a "defaults from X.msh.opt" chip with a one-click Reset. Mirror the existing auto-association rule for `<volume>_LUT.txt` in §7.6. Phase 2. Same treatment for `<mesh>.geo` / `*.pos` electrode-position views (`m2m_ernie/eeg_positions/*.geo`, `ernie_seeg_views.pos`) — at minimum parse `.csv` electrode files into the points layer, since that is the format SimNIBS writes.

findings.title: No vector-field glyphs — E-fields can only be shown as a magnitude scalar
findings.claim: `Field` carries `ncomp: 1|3|9` and `MeshLayer.field.component: 'mag'|0|1|2`, so a 3-component E-field can only be collapsed to a scalar and colour-mapped. There is no arrow/glyph rendering and no streamlines anywhere in the contract. The user's requirement names electric fields explicitly, and direction is the physically meaningful half of a TI/tDCS field — it is why SimNIBS's own sidecar sets `General.VectorType = 1` / `View[0].VectorType = 1`, i.e. Gmsh renders these as arrows by default. "Take inspiration from Gmsh" and then dropping Gmsh's vector display is a visible regression for the primary data type.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:107 (`component:'mag'|0|1|2`), :185 ("Vector fields keep ncomp=3"); grep for "glyph|arrow|streamline|VectorType" across docs/ returns nothing. `General.VectorType = 1;` in m2m_ernie/ernie.msh.opt and `View[0].VectorType = 1; View[0].CenterGlyphs = 1; View[0].GlyphLocation = 1;` in docs_example_TI.msh.opt. AGENTS.md:13 lists "element fields incl. `TI_max`, vector `E`" as required test data.
findings.fix: Add `MeshLayer.glyphs?: { field: {source,name}, shape:'arrow'|'line', subsample: number|{everyNth}|{maxCount}, scale: 'fixed'|'byMagnitude', lengthMm, colorBy:'magnitude'|'solid', clipToCutPlane: boolean }` and render with one instanced draw (a shared cone+shaft VAO, per-instance origin/direction/magnitude) in the opaque pass — no new geometry from WASM, so it costs one buffer upload. Restrict glyph origins to the currently visible tags and, when a cut plane is active, to elements the plane intersects (that is the Gmsh look and it caps the instance count). Phase 2, alongside the mesh field layer. Streamlines/tractography stay out of v1 — say so in §1 non-goals.

findings.title: Atlases have no per-region visibility, no searchable region list, and no jump-to-structure
findings.claim: `VolumeLayer` gets `labelLut`, `labelMode:'fill'|'outline'|'both'`, `outlineWidthPx` — all-or-nothing rendering of every label in the file. The single most common atlas operation is "show me only the left thalamus" (or three structures), which requires per-label visibility; the second is "where is the superior temporal gyrus" — a searchable region list that jumps the cursor to a structure. The contract's only nod to region names is one word in §8's info panel. `labeling.nii.gz` with `labeling_LUT.txt` and the HCP_MMP1 annot (360 regions) are unusable as browsers without this. The user asked for "import regions and atlases in colors and outlines", which is a workflow, not a colormap.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:104 (VolumeLayer label fields), :273-275 (§8 info panel: "label name"). Test data: m2m_ernie/segmentation/labeling.nii.gz + labeling_LUT.txt, m2m_ernie/final_tissues.nii.gz + final_tissues_LUT.txt (14 entries incl. `100 Electrode`, `500 Saline_or_gel` — note non-contiguous ids, so an id-indexed array is wrong), rh.ernie_HCP_MMP1.annot. `MeshLayer.isolate.labelVolume` already assumes a caller can name specific `labels: number[]`, but nothing in the UI produces that list.
findings.fix: Add `visibleLabels?: Uint32Array` (null = all) and `labelOpacity?: Record<number, number>` to `VolumeLayer`, and a `Region` panel in §8: search-as-you-type over the LUT/LabelTable, per-row eye + colour swatch + voxel-count, `Alt+click` a row to solo it, double-click to move the cursor to that label's centroid (or largest connected component's centroid — add `pub fn label_centroids(vol) -> Vec<(u32,[f32;3],u64)>` to §6.3). Wire the same selection into `MeshLayer.isolate.labelVolume.labels` so "isolate mesh to this ROI" is one click. Store LUT entries in a map keyed by id, not an array indexed by id (ids reach 500 with gaps). Phase 2.

findings.title: No typed coordinate entry, no copy-coordinate, no second coordinate space in the readout
findings.claim: The cursor is set only by clicking or arrow-nudging (§7.5). There is no box to type a coordinate into and no way to copy the current one out. Reproducing a reported peak ("MNI −42, 18, 6"), checking a coordinate a collaborator emailed, and pasting a coordinate into a methods section are daily operations, and every comparable tool has the box. The info panel also shows only subject RAS + per-layer voxel indices; there is no MNI/template column, even though the subject tree carries the forward warp to MNI. Without it, users bounce back to Freeview for the one thing they do most often.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:273-275 (info panel contents), :258-260 (interaction: click, arrows, PgUp/PgDn — no coordinate entry). Freeview's Measure tool documentation explicitly reports "the intensities and RAS coordinates of voxels which the drawn line intersects", and the FreeSurfer CoordinateSystems page treats scanner RAS / tkrRAS / MNI305 as coordinates users routinely convert between. Test data has the warp: m2m_ernie/toMNI/ and m2m_ernie/T1_ernie_MNI.nii.gz.
findings.fix: §8: add a coordinate bar above the info panel — an editable `x y z` field with a space selector (`World RAS` | `Voxel (active layer)` | `MNI`), Enter jumps the cursor, a copy button puts `-42.0 18.0 6.0` on the clipboard, and paste accepts comma- or space-separated triples. §3: define an optional per-dataset `toTemplate?: { name:'MNI152'|'MNI305', kind:'affine', matrix: mat4 }` (affine only in v1; state that nonlinear warps are out of scope) and show the MNI column in the readout when one is loaded. Phase 1 for the RAS/voxel box (it is a `setCursor` call), Phase 2 for the MNI column.

findings.title: Info panel reports only the clicked cursor — no live hover readout
findings.claim: §8's info panel shows "cursor RAS + per-layer voxel index / value / label name / element id / tag / field values". §7.5 sets the cursor on click. There is no mouse-hover readout, so inspecting a field means clicking at every point of interest, which also moves all three slice planes and destroys your view position. Freeview shows Cursor and Mouse as two simultaneous sections precisely so you can sweep the mouse over a map and read values without committing. This is the primary way people read a stat map, and its absence will be the first complaint. It also has an architectural consequence: hover probing of a tet mesh needs `mesh_locate` at pointer-move rate, which the latest-wins scheduler must be specified to handle (drop, not queue) and which needs the point locator built eagerly at load, not lazily on first probe.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:273-275, :258-259. Freeview interface docs: "The bottom of the window displays 'Cursor/Mouse sections' … As you move the mouse over the display window, coordinates and data about the voxel under the cursor appear." §6.3 provides `locate_point(mesh, grid, p)` but §6.4/§5 never say when `PointLocator` is built or that probes are latest-wins.
findings.fix: §8: split the info panel into `Cursor` (last click, persistent) and `Mouse` (live, updates on pointermove, blank when the pointer leaves a view) with identical row structure. Volume values resolve on the UI thread from the retained typed array (§5 already keeps it there) — zero latency. Mesh element probes go through `mesh_locate` as a latest-wins op with its own op key so it never queues behind a cut; build `PointLocator` during load (add it to the §9 load budget) and state a target: hover readout updated within 16 ms for volumes and 50 ms for meshes. Phase 2 with the probing bullet.

findings.title: Window/level has no histogram — the stats are computed and then thrown away
findings.claim: `VolumeDataset.stats` includes a 256-bin histogram and seven percentiles, and §6.1 requires the reader to compute them, but §8's UX contract never surfaces them. Window/level is therefore only reachable by right-drag — a blind gesture with no feedback about where the data actually lives. For E-field and stat maps, where the interesting range is a thin tail (TI_max is essentially all below 0.13 V/m with a long tail), dragging blind is genuinely hard, which is why SimNIBS precomputes the 99.9th-percentile range for Gmsh rather than letting users find it. Freeview's per-layer Configure panel is built around exactly this histogram-with-draggable-handles widget.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:82 (`histogram: Float32Array(256)`, percentiles), :167-168 (§6.1 requires them), :272-276 (§8 lists panels; no histogram). `View[0].CustomMax = 0.12217871837158231` in docs_example_TI.msh.opt is SimNIBS's precomputed high percentile of the TI_max field, shipped because a blind range is unusable.
findings.fix: §8: add a histogram widget to the volume and mesh-field property editors — log-y toggle, draggable window handles and threshold handles drawn on it, the current colormap painted along the x axis, and one-click presets (`min–max`, `2–98%`, `p50–p99.9`, `symmetric ±p99`). Add `'99.9'` to the percentile set in §4/§6.1 (E-fields need it; 99 is too low). Same widget for `Field.stats` on mesh layers. Phase 2, with the volume-slice-layer bullet.

findings.title: Mesh-cut-on-slice (the Gmsh look on 2D views) has no performance budget and no acceleration structure
findings.claim: `MeshLayer.fillIn2D` draws tet cut polygons on the 2D slices — the feature the requirement calls cross-section visualization. But §9's slice-scrub row budgets only "T1 + 2 overlays + label outlines", and the cut row only covers "cut-plane drag". Scrubbing a slice with `fillIn2D` on triggers `plane_cut` over 5.9 M tets three times per slice change (one per plane), through a `Cut` that also builds `edge_segments` and `boundary_segments`. §6.3 specifies `plane_cut(mesh, topo, plane, mask)` with no spatial index at all — it is a linear scan of every tet per cut. At 60 fps that is ~1 G tet-plane tests per second single-threaded in WASM. The headline feature will run at single-digit fps and there is no budget in the contract that would catch it.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:110 (`fillIn2D`), :194 (`plane_cut` signature — no index parameter), :288-291 (§9 rows: "Cut-plane drag (cap recompute + upload) ≥ 30 fps", "Slice scrub with T1 + 2 overlays + label outlines 60 fps" — no row combining the two), :132 ("single-threaded v1; rayon-ready"). Field size measured: docs_example_TI.msh carries one `$ElementData` ("TI_max", 1 component, 5,899,838 elements, f64) starting at byte 184,207,351 of a 255,005,467-byte file.
findings.fix: Add to §6.3 a `PlaneIndex` built once per mesh at load — tet AABBs bucketed along each of the three canonical axes (a sorted min/max interval list per axis suffices for canonical planes; a coarse uniform grid for oblique) so a canonical cut touches only the O(n^2/3) tets straddling the plane. Change the signature to `plane_cut(mesh, topo, index: &PlaneIndex, plane, mask)`. Add a §9 row: "Slice scrub with T1 + Thalamus_TI.msh fillIn2D + contours (5.9 M tets) — 30 fps, cut latency < 25 ms". Add a cached-cut policy: when only `offset` changes along a fixed normal, reuse the straddle candidate set. Decide this in Phase 1 (it changes the crate API), verify in Phase 2.

findings.title: Screenshot contract is too weak for figures, and the headless render path is never exposed
findings.claim: §8 offers "PNG of one view or the whole grid at 1×/2×/4× DPR". Journals ask for an exact pixel width or a DPI at a physical size, not a multiplier of whatever the window happens to be. There is no transparent-background option, no option to suppress the crosshair/annotations, no auto-trim, and no statement about whether the colour bar and orientation labels are included. Separately, §4 says the `ViewSpec` exists so a scene "can be saved, reloaded, and rendered headlessly" — but no CLI or API ever exposes that, so batch figure generation over 30 subjects (the thing that would beat Freeview outright) is unreachable. Freeview has shipped `-ss <file> <magnification> <auto-trim>` for years and people script it constantly.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:278 (screenshot spec), :116 ("rendered headlessly"), :277 (CLI args are only `tetravox file1.nii.gz mesh.msh`). ROADMAP.md:22 (Phase 2 screenshot) and :28 (packaging) never mention a headless mode. Freeview mailing-list threads on "Freeview command line option for multiple screenshots" document `-ss` with magnification.
findings.fix: §8: `screenshot({ target:'view'|'grid', width?: px, height?: px, scale?: number, dpi?: number, background:'scene'|'white'|'transparent', include:{ colorbar, orientationLabels, crosshair, cornerInfo, scaleBar }, autoTrim: boolean })` → PNG with the DPI written into the pHYs chunk. Add a CLI in Phase 3 that is really a Phase-2 side effect: `tetravox --scene s.tetravox.json --screenshot out.png --width 2400 --background white [--headless]`, running the same engine in an offscreen Electron window. Also specify `.tetravox.json` path semantics now (paths stored relative to the scene file with an absolute fallback, and a "relocate missing dataset" dialog on load) — otherwise saved scenes break the first time anyone moves a folder.

findings.title: `EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2` is disabled by default in Chromium, so the §7.1 Timer and the status bar's frame-ms will silently report nothing
findings.claim: §7.1 specifies a `Timer` wrapper around `EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2` "when available", §8 puts frame ms and GPU memory in the status bar, and §9 makes GPU timings a release gate. Chromium disabled the timer-query extensions by default over Rowhammer/timing-attack concerns and re-enabled them only behind `chrome://flags/#enable-webgl-developer-extensions`. In a packaged Electron app that flag is off, so `getExtension` returns null on every user's machine and on CI — the benchmark harness and the status bar will report zeros, and nobody will notice because the code path is guarded by "when available".
findings.evidence: Chromium discussion threads and the MDN compat data issue for EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2 record that the timer extensions were disabled due to potential rowhammer use and re-enabled only via the `enable-webgl-developer-extensions` developer flag. ARCHITECTURE.md:225 (Timer "when available"), :276 (status bar frame ms / GPU memory), :293 ("CI records them as artefacts").
findings.fix: §7.1: state that the engine reports two numbers — CPU frame time from rAF deltas (always available, this is what the status bar shows) and GPU time from the timer query, available only when the app is launched with the extension enabled. In `packages/app` main, call `app.commandLine.appendSwitch('enable-webgl-developer-extensions')` and note it in DECISIONS.md; have `scripts/bench.ts` fail loudly ("GPU timing unavailable") rather than printing 0. Also drop "GPU memory estimate" from the status bar or relabel it "estimated" — WebGL2 has no memory-query extension in Chromium, so it can only ever be a sum of your own allocations.

findings.title: Drag-and-drop file paths: `File.path` no longer exists in modern Electron
findings.claim: §8 promises drag-and-drop opening and §5 routes file reads through Electron main by path. The classic way to get that path in the renderer — the non-standard `File.path` property Electron added — was deprecated and removed in Electron 32. The replacement is `webUtils.getPathForFile(file)`, which must be called in the preload and exposed over `contextBridge` (it is not available in a sandboxed renderer), and it has known failure modes with bundlers and with certain macOS drop sources. If this is discovered during Phase 1 implementation it is a preload/IPC redesign rather than a one-line change.
findings.evidence: electron/electron PR #42053 "feat: remove File.path" and issues #44370 / #44600 / #45540 document the removal, the `webUtils.getPathForFile()` replacement, its webpack breakage, and cases where it resolves to an empty path for dropped files. ARCHITECTURE.md:277 (drag-and-drop), :124-127 (main does fs read by path).
findings.fix: §5/§8: specify the drop path explicitly — preload exposes `getDroppedFilePath(file)` wrapping `webUtils.getPathForFile`, and the renderer falls back to reading the `File` object's bytes directly (no native gunzip, WASM miniz_oxide inflate) when the path comes back empty. Add a Phase-0 E2E test that drops a `.nii.gz` and a `.msh` onto the window and asserts both load, so the fallback is exercised from day one. Note the Electron major version the contract targets in §1.

findings.title: Layout set and 4D handling are thinner than the tools being replaced
findings.claim: Layouts are `1x1`, `1x3`, `2x2`, `3d-only`. Freeview also ships `1x3 horizontal` (large pane with three on the right), which is what people use on wide monitors, and NiiVue supports a mosaic/lightbox layout (`sliceMosaicString`) — a grid of many slices at once, which is the standard QC view for checking a segmentation or a registration across a whole volume. Separately, `VolumeLayer.volumeIndex` exists and `nvols` is parsed, but §8 gives no control for it, so a 4D file loads and strands the user on volume 0.
findings.evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md:255-256 (layouts), :102 (`volumeIndex`), :79 (`nvols`), :24 (4D playback a non-goal but "loading a 4D NIfTI and picking a volume index is in scope"). Freeview interface docs list "1x3 horizontal". NiiVue exposes `sliceMosaicString` for mosaic layouts (niivue.com/docs/options).
findings.fix: Add `1x3-horizontal` to §7.5's layouts (trivial — same view set, different grid) and a `mosaic` layout in Phase 3 parameterised by `{ plane, startMm, stepMm, rows, cols }`, reusing the existing slice quad draw. Add to §8 a volume-index spinner + slider in the layer editor, shown only when `nvols > 1`, with `,`/`.` to step — this is the whole cost of honouring the in-scope half of the 4D non-goal.

reviews.verdict: The architecture is unusually strong on the hard parts — the worker/WASM split, sort-based topology, exact CPU cut caps plus GPU discard, latest-wins scheduling, and the insistence on screenshot-verified rendering are all the right calls, and the crate API contracts are specific enough to build against. What it is missing is almost entirely the layer between "the pixels are correct" and "a scientist can work in this": the contract has no orientation labels or slice annotation on 2D views (a laterality hazard given the global radiological toggle), no colour bar until Phase 3, no active-layer concept, no per-tissue opacity (which the user asked for by name), no vector glyphs for the E-fields that are the primary data, no way to display the .annot parcellations the test data ships, no load progress or cancel for the 250-500 MB meshes that are routine here, and no heatscale/histogram/coordinate-entry affordances that Freeview users reach for hourly. Fixing these is mostly data-model and UX-contract work that must land before Phase 2 code is written — three of them (per-tag style, label colour mode, plane-cut spatial index) change crate and layer signatures, so they are cheap now and expensive after Phase 2 starts.

findings.title: plane_cut is a full O(N) scan — the ≥30 fps cut-plane drag target is unreachable as designed
findings.claim: `plane_cut(mesh, topo, plane, mask)` has no spatial index, so dragging the plane rescans all 4,722,625 ernie tets every frame. §9 demands ≥30 fps end-to-end (33 ms for scan + polygon extraction + node-field interpolation + copy-out + transfer + VBO upload). The scan alone eats the whole budget. This is the marquee Gmsh-inspired feature and the one most likely to feel laggy.
findings.evidence: Measured proxy of exactly the scan (4.72 M tets, 847,165 nodes, 4-node gather + 4 dot products per tet, bitmask test, spatially clustered indices) in V8 typed arrays: 290.7 ms per scan, stable over repeats (289.1 ms avg of 3). Even assuming a tight Rust/WASM SIMD version is 3–5× faster, that is 60–100 ms → 10–16 fps, before any of the other five stages. Element composition verified by parsing $Elements of /Users/idohaber/datasets/000/derivatives/SimNIBS/sub-ernie/m2m_ernie/ernie.msh: {type 2: 1,177,213 tris, type 4: 4,722,625 tets}.
findings.fix: Add a spatial index to tvx-geom and make it part of load, not of the cut: bucket tets into a uniform grid with per-cell AABBs (reuse the `PointLocator` grid §6.3 already specifies) so a plane visits only O(N^(2/3)) cells. Change the signature to `plane_cut(mesh, index: &TetGrid, plane: &Plane, mask: &BitMask) -> Cut` and add `build_tet_grid(mesh) -> TetGrid` to §6.3 with its own perf target (< 500 ms WASM for ernie). Also specify the upload path the contract currently omits: caps go into a pre-sized, double-buffered VBO written with `bufferSubData` (orphan + sub-update), never a fresh `bufferData` per frame. Add a drag/settle contract: coarse cap while the gizmo is held, exact cap on release.

findings.title: Building TetTopology on load is unnecessary for the first frame and blows the memory bar
findings.claim: `tag_surfaces(mesh, topo)` takes topology, so the load path must build it — but ernie.msh already ships the tissue boundary as 1,177,213 tagged tri elements (tags 1001,1002,1003,1005–1010,1099). The default 3D look needs zero tet topology. Building it anyway costs ~265 MB resident plus ~300 MB of radix scratch on top of 184 MB of input bytes and 124 MB of mesh arrays — ~875 MB peak for the file §9 budgets at < 1.5 GB, with no headroom for the 396 MB and 255 MB meshes that exist in the same test dataset.
findings.evidence: Parsed $Elements directly: tris 1,177,213 with surface tags 1001–1010/1099; tets 4,722,625 with tissue tags 1–10. Memory model from those counts: nodes 10.2 MB, tets 75.6 + 18.9 MB, tris 14.1 + 4.7 MB; unique faces ≈ 4,722,625×4/2 = 9.4 M → faces 113 MB + face_tets 76 MB + tet_faces 76 MB = 265 MB; sort scratch 18,890,500 keys × 16 B = 302 MB; input file 184 MB (not the 176 MB §6.2 states). `ls` in the dataset: flex_20260709_*_TI.msh = 396,601,700 B and Thalamus_TI.msh = 255,005,467 B.
findings.fix: Change §6.3 to `tag_surfaces(mesh) -> Vec<(tag, Faces)>` built from the existing tri elements; make `build_topology` lazy, triggered only by the first `boundary_faces`/`isolate` call, and say so in §5's load flow. Require the parser to drop the input byte buffer (and the gzip inflate buffer) before returning. Add to §9 an explicit peak-WASM-heap budget per file size, and state the constraint the contract currently ignores: `WebAssembly.Memory` grows but never shrinks, so the worker's high-water mark persists across loads — either recreate the worker on `free(handle)` of a large mesh or budget for the largest file ever opened in the session.

findings.title: 6 clip planes via fragment `discard` is the wrong primitive — WEBGL_clip_cull_distance is available and 28% faster
findings.claim: §7.4 mandates `discard` on the clipped side. `discard` defeats early-Z and forces late depth resolution on Apple's TBDR, and the cost compounds with the transparent pass and the pick pass. WebGL2 exposes hardware clip planes, with exactly enough of them.
findings.evidence: Chromium / ANGLE (Apple, ANGLE Metal Renderer: Apple M2 Max), 1,180,980 de-indexed triangles, 2880×1620, 4×MSAA, same scene and session: 6-plane fragment `discard` = 2.89 ms/frame; 6-plane `gl_ClipDistance` = 2.07 ms/frame. `gl.getSupportedExtensions()` on that context lists WEBGL_clip_cull_distance with MAX_CLIP_DISTANCES_WEBGL = 8 (≥ the 6 required) and MAX_CULL_DISTANCES_WEBGL = 0. Compile gotcha verified: `gl_ClipDistance[i]` in a loop without redeclaration fails — "The gl_ClipDistance array must be sized by the shader either redeclaring it with a size or indexing it only with constant integral expressions"; `out highp float gl_ClipDistance[6];` with unrolled constant indices links fine.
findings.fix: §7.4: clipping is `gl_ClipDistance` when WEBGL_clip_cull_distance is present, with the `discard` shader as an explicit fallback path. §7.1's `Program` needs a shader chunk emitting `#extension GL_ANGLE_clip_cull_distance : require` + `out highp float gl_ClipDistance[6];` with unrolled assignments, and the GL kit must track `gl.enable(ext.CLIP_DISTANCE0_WEBGL + i)` as render state. Do not plan on cull distances (0 on Metal).

findings.title: The GPU format table has no filterable 16-bit path — costing 2–5× in upload time and VRAM on the actual data
findings.claim: `format: 'R8'|'R16UI'|'R32F'|'RGBA8'` forces int16 scalars (T1) to either R32F (2× memory, 3× upload) or R16UI (no linear filtering — `interpolation:'linear'` in VolumeLayer becomes unimplementable). Float volumes at 512³ land in R32F and produce a multi-frame stall. §7.3 also silently depends on OES_texture_float_linear without naming it — R32F is not a texture-filterable format in core WebGL2.
findings.evidence: Measured `texImage3D` + `finish()` on M2 Max/ANGLE-Metal: T1 at 256×256×208 as R32F = 55 MB, 9.2 ms; the same data as R16 via EXT_texture_norm16 = 27 MB, 3.3 ms. label_prep at 512×512×416 as R16UI = 218 MB, 34.9 ms; as R32F = 436 MB, 174.1 ms. Both extensions are present on this context (OES_texture_float_linear, EXT_texture_norm16) and R32F LINEAR verified to actually interpolate (texels 0.0/1.0 sampled at the midpoint returned 128 with LINEAR, 255 with NEAREST). MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE = 2048. Header dims read from the dataset: m2m_ernie/T1.nii.gz is 256×256×208 int16 (§9 says "256³"); label_prep/T1_upsampled.nii.gz and tissue_labeling_upsampled.nii.gz are 512×512×416.
findings.fix: Extend the format enum to `R8 | R8UI | R16 | R16UI | R16F | R32F | RGBA8` and make §6.1's `gpu_payload` pick the narrowest format that represents the data exactly and is filterable when `interpolation:'linear'` is possible (int16 → R16 normalized + a scale/offset uniform; labels → R16UI/R8UI nearest; float → R16F when the range permits, R32F otherwise). §7.1 must request OES_texture_float_linear and EXT_texture_norm16 and §7.3 must state the fallback when either is absent. Add a rule that any texture over ~32 MB uploads via chunked `texSubImage3D` slabs budgeted across frames, and add a `MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE` validation + downsample path so a >2048 dimension fails loudly instead of at draw time.

findings.title: Label outlines derived from dFdx of world position break at both zoom extremes
findings.claim: "compare the label at ±1 screen pixel along the two in-plane axes (using dFdx/dFdy of the world position)" ties the sampling step to screen scale. Zoomed in, one screen pixel is far smaller than a voxel, every tap lands in the same voxel and the outline disappears. Zoomed out, one screen pixel spans several voxels, taps skip label runs and the outline breaks up. The atlas-outline feature the user explicitly asked for is only correct at one zoom level.
findings.evidence: Direct consequence of the specified formula: the tap offset is `dFdx(worldPos)`, whose magnitude is (world extent of the view)/(pixels), independent of voxel size. The dataset makes both regimes routine: segmentation/labeling.nii.gz is 1 mm, label_prep/tissue_labeling_upsampled.nii.gz is 0.5 mm, and a 2D view zoomed to a thalamic ROI puts ~0.05 mm per screen pixel. Cost is not the obstacle — measured 3-layer slice compositing at 2880×1620 was 1.10 ms with a 4-tap outline and 1.23 ms with 8 taps, so extra taps are affordable.
findings.fix: Define the outline in voxel space and the width in screen space: detect the boundary with 4 (or 8) taps at exactly ±1 voxel along the two in-plane voxel axes, then set the drawn thickness from `outlineWidthPx * (world units per screen pixel)` compared against the distance to that boundary, i.e. tap offset = `inPlaneVoxelAxis * max(1.0, outlineWidthPx * pxInVoxels)`. State the minification story too: integer 3D textures cannot be mipmapped or filtered, so when a screen pixel covers many voxels either supersample the label taps or precompute an R8 boundary volume in the worker.

findings.title: Coplanar slice layers on LEQUAL + no depth write is not guaranteed to composite; and the single-pass alternative is impossible in WebGL2
findings.claim: "One quad draw per (layer, plane); overlays use depthFunc(LEQUAL) + no depth write so they sit on the base slice" assumes coplanar quads produce identical interpolated depth. They will not: each layer's quad is sized to its own volume's extent, so the vertex data differs and the ES invariance rules (identical results only for identical inputs and identical shaders) do not cover it. The result is intermittent, view-dependent dropout of overlay layers. The review question of one-quad-per-layer vs a single N-layer shader is also settled in a way the contract does not record.
findings.evidence: OpenGL ES 3.0 invariance only guarantees bit-identical results for identical vertex data through identical shaders; two coplanar quads of different extent violate that. Separately, a single-pass N-layer shader is not expressible: on ANGLE/Metal WebGL2, `uniform sampler3D u[4]; texture(u[i], v)` with a non-const `i` fails to compile — "ERROR: 0:4: '[' : array index for samplers must be constant integral expressions" — and the same for a loop over `sampler3D u[8]`; only a constant index compiles. So single-pass would need one shader permutation per layer count. Perf does not decide it either: single-pass 3 layers = 1.10 ms vs quad-per-layer 3 draws = 1.04 ms at 2880×1620.
findings.fix: Record quad-per-layer as the decision with the real reason (ESSL 3.00 forbids dynamically indexed sampler arrays) in DECISIONS.md, and fix the depth story explicitly in §7.3: (a) in 2D views draw all slice layers with DEPTH_TEST disabled, order = layer order; (b) in the 3D view all layers of one plane share one quad geometry — the plane's, not any volume's — with a single depth-writing prepass, so depth is identical by construction; (c) given the mm-scale scene, use EXT_clip_control (present on this context) for zero-to-one depth + reverse-Z on the 3D depth buffer.

findings.title: Oblique slices are claimed as supported but have no representation in the data model or ViewSpec
findings.claim: §3 says "oblique slices are supported by the same shader path; the three canonical views are just fixed planes", but `Scene = { datasets, layers, views: ViewLayout, cursor: vec3, ... }` carries no plane normal, no in-plane up vector, and no per-view offset, and `VolumeLayer.showIn3D` has no plane definition either. ROADMAP then defers oblique to Phase 3. So v1 ships a serialisable ViewSpec that cannot express the feature, and every Phase 1–2 consumer written against three fixed axes (cursor sync, `wheel = slice ±1`, PgUp/PgDn, radiological toggle, screenshot, 2D cameras with "fixed orientation, pan/zoom only") gets rewritten in Phase 3.
findings.evidence: Read of §3, §4 (`Scene`), §7.5 ("2D cameras are orthographic with fixed orientation (pan/zoom only)") and ROADMAP Phase 3 ("Oblique slice view") — the three statements are mutually inconsistent. `ClipPlane { normal, offset, enabled }` exists but only inside `MeshLayer.clip`, never for volume slices.
findings.fix: Put the plane in the model now, in Phase 1: `interface SliceView { mode:'axial'|'coronal'|'sagittal'|'oblique'; normal: vec3; up: vec3; offset: number }` on each 2D view, with the canonical modes as presets that lock normal/up. Define slice stepping as ±1 voxel along the normal of the topmost volume layer (so it is already correct for oblique), give 2D cameras an in-plane roll, and build the slice quad as the plane clipped to the union of visible layer bounds rather than to one volume's face. That same SliceView is the geometry for `showIn3D` planes, so it removes duplicated work rather than adding any.

findings.title: No antialiasing strategy, and the pick and OIT passes silently lose whatever MSAA the default framebuffer had
findings.claim: 1.18 M triangles over a ~1 M-pixel head silhouette means most tissue triangles are sub-pixel; without MSAA the surfaces will crawl and shimmer under orbit, which is the single most visible quality difference from Gmsh/MeshLab. The contract never mentions `antialias`, MSAA samples, or FXAA. Worse, §7.2's pick pass (and Phase-3 WBOIT) render into their own FBOs, where the canvas's `antialias:true` does not apply — that needs multisampled renderbuffers plus a `blitFramebuffer` resolve, and an integer pick target cannot be meaningfully multisampled at all, so pick results and displayed pixels disagree at every silhouette edge.
findings.evidence: On the test context `MAX_SAMPLES` = 4 and `MAX_DRAW_BUFFERS` = 8; `OES_draw_buffers_indexed` present. RGBA32UI pick FBO verified: `checkFramebufferStatus` complete, `IMPLEMENTATION_COLOR_READ_TYPE` = UNSIGNED_INT, `readPixels(RGBA_INTEGER, UNSIGNED_INT)` returns without error, and a 1×1 readback costs 0.043 ms — so a synchronous pick is fine and needs no PBO. Triangle count 1,180,980 rendered at 2880×1620 in the benchmark above.
findings.fix: Specify the framebuffer chain in §7.1: 4×MSAA colour + depth renderbuffers → `blitFramebuffer` resolve → overlay/post → canvas, with sample count as a quality setting. State that the pick pass renders single-sample at 1× DPR into its own RGBA32UI FBO, and that picking takes the nearest non-zero ID within a small radius to absorb the resolve mismatch.

findings.title: The pick pass as specified cannot produce the 3D hit point that §7.5 requires
findings.claim: §7.2's pick FBO encodes `(layer, primitive)` only, but §7.5 says "double-click = pick (sets cursor to hit point)" — and the cursor is a world point that drives all three slice planes. There is no depth or position channel to recover it from, and WebGL2 cannot `readPixels` a depth attachment.
findings.evidence: WebGL2 restricts `readPixels` to RGBA / RGBA_INTEGER and the implementation-defined format; DEPTH_COMPONENT is not a legal read format, so depth cannot be read back from the pick FBO. §7.2 lists only `(layer, primitive)` as the encoded payload. Recovering the point from the primitive id alone would require a CPU-side ray/triangle intersection the contract does not specify either.
findings.fix: Use all four channels of the RGBA32UI target — `.x = layerId`, `.y = primitiveId`, `.zw = floatBitsToUint` of NDC depth (or window-space z) — and unproject on readback; or add a second MRT attachment carrying world position as RGBA32F (EXT_color_buffer_float is present, MAX_DRAW_BUFFERS = 8). State which in §7.2 and add the unprojection to the engine API so cursor-from-pick is a defined operation.

findings.title: Where de-indexing happens is unspecified, and de-indexing unconditionally is the wrong default
findings.claim: Flat per-face scalars and barycentric wireframe both require de-indexed geometry, but `tag_surfaces` returns `{indices, owner_tet}` (indexed) while `plane_cut` returns de-indexed positions — and nothing says who expands the surface. If it happens on the UI thread it is a multi-hundred-millisecond hitch that violates AGENTS rule 6. And it is unnecessary for the default look: `colorMode:'tag'` is per-tissue (one uniform colour per tag) and node-field colouring is smooth, so neither needs de-indexing.
findings.evidence: Expanding ernie's 1,177,213 surface tris to 3,542,940 vertices with position+normal+scalar+barycentric measured 142 MB of attribute data. Element tags confirm tag colouring is per-tissue, not per-face: only 10 distinct surface tags across those 1.18 M triangles. Raster cost is not the issue — the de-indexed 1.18 M-triangle draw with barycentric wireframe and 4×MSAA at 2880×1620 measured 2.24 ms on M2 Max, and 2.32 ms without the wireframe.
findings.fix: State in §6.4/§7.4 that de-indexing happens in the worker and arrives as transferables, and that the engine keeps two geometry variants per mesh layer: indexed (default — one draw call per tag with a uniform colour, plus node-field colouring) and de-indexed (built lazily on first use of `field.source === 'elm'` or `edges: true`). Note the consequence in the UX contract: toggling `MeshLayer.edges` or switching to an element field is a load with a progress state, not a free uniform flip. Per-tag sub-draws also make `tagVisibility` free.

findings.title: Barycentric wireframe draws the triangulation, not the element — the exact artefact Gmsh does not have
findings.claim: "Element edges: barycentric-coordinate wireframe in the fragment shader (no extra draw call)" marks all three edges of every triangle. A tet's cut polygon is a quadrilateral split into two triangles, so the wireframe will draw the artificial diagonal across every quad cap face. `element isolation` and "cut-through" views — the two features taken from Gmsh — are precisely where this shows.
findings.evidence: §6.3's `Cut` already returns `edge_segments: Vec<f32>` described as "polygon outlines for element edges", which means the design already knows the barycentric path is insufficient for caps — but §7.4 then specifies barycentric as the element-edge mechanism with no statement of which applies where. A plane cutting a tet yields a triangle or a quad; the quad case is roughly half of intersected tets.
findings.fix: Split the contract: cut caps draw their edges from `Cut.edge_segments` line geometry (already specified) and never use barycentric; surface wireframe uses barycentric with a per-vertex 3-component edge mask so non-original edges are suppressed. Add `edge_mask: Vec<u8>` (3 bits per triangle) to the de-indexed surface payload in §6.3/§6.4 so the shader can zero out suppressed edges.

findings.title: Per-object back-to-front transparency fails for the exact surfaces this app shows, and MeshLayer forbids the cheap fix
findings.claim: "sorted by layer order then back-to-front per object" is correct only for convex or well-separated objects. A semi-transparent cortical surface is deeply non-convex — gyri and sulci self-overlap in every view direction — so a single sorted draw of one GM surface is visibly wrong, which is the most common thing a user will do (translucent skin over a field-coloured cortex). Weighted-blended OIT in Phase 3 is depth-weighted and washes out exactly this high-contrast layered case. Separately, §7.2 puts cut caps in the opaque pass, which is wrong when the owning mesh layer has `opacity < 1`.
findings.evidence: ernie's surface tags are ten nested but individually non-convex shells (1001 scalp 249,245 tris; 1002 skull 335,930; 1005 GM 77,032; 1007 143,499; 1008 158,262 — counts from parsing $Elements). MeshLayer as specified has `backfaceCull: boolean`, which admits only a single-pass draw and forecloses the two-pass fix.
findings.fix: For v1, specify the two-pass draw for closed transparent surfaces — `cullFace(FRONT)` then `cullFace(BACK)` — which is exactly correct for a closed manifold and removes the worst artefact for ~10 lines. Change `backfaceCull: boolean` to `faceMode: 'cull' | 'both' | 'twoPassSorted'` so the model can express it. Move caps into whichever pass their owning layer is in. If WBOIT still lands in Phase 3, note that OES_draw_buffers_indexed and MAX_DRAW_BUFFERS = 8 are available for the accumulation/revealage targets.

findings.title: "Lagless" has no mechanism: render-on-demand is specified without a frame pump, interaction quality, or adaptive fallback
findings.claim: "Render only on demand (requestRender() after any state change) — never a free-running loop" is the right instinct but is the whole of the contract. There is no statement that renders coalesce to one per requestAnimationFrame (a 120 Hz trackpad orbit fires more pointer events than vsyncs), no interaction-vs-idle quality split, no settle behaviour, and no definition of what the status bar's "fps, frame ms" measures when nothing is rendering. The headline user requirement — "high-performance and lagless" — is the one thing with no mechanism behind it.
findings.evidence: §7.2 and §8 read together: the only guidance is `requestRender()` plus a status bar showing fps/frame ms. §9's targets are steady-state throughput numbers, which a dirty-flag renderer can satisfy while still feeling laggy (input latency, one-frame-behind cursor, a 174 ms texture upload or a 290 ms plane scan landing inside a gesture).
findings.fix: Specify in §7.2: a single rAF-driven pump that coalesces all dirty flags into at most one render per frame; an `interacting` state entered on pointer-down/wheel and left ~100 ms after the last input, which selects reduced quality (1× DPR, MSAA off, wireframe off, decimated caps, coarse volume filtering) and triggers a full-quality re-render on settle; and a hard rule that no single main-thread call inside a gesture may exceed ~4 ms (which is what forces the chunked texture upload in §7.3 and the async cap path in §6.3). Add input-latency (pointer-to-photon) to §9 alongside throughput.

findings.title: "Ships Chromium ⇒ identical WebGL2 on macOS/Linux" is false, and the §9 numbers are quoted for the best machine in the family
findings.claim: The Electron-over-Tauri rationale asserts GPU parity that Chromium does not provide: it blocklists many Linux GPU/driver combinations and falls back to SwiftShader silently, and Wayland needs explicit ozone flags. The design now depends on three *extensions* (OES_texture_float_linear, EXT_texture_norm16, WEBGL_clip_cull_distance) that are present on ANGLE/Metal but not guaranteed on Mesa, llvmpipe, or older Intel. Meanwhile "60 fps (≤ 8 ms) on Apple M-series" quotes a family spanning roughly 4× in GPU throughput. And Phase 0 plans pixel assertions with "swiftshader ok", so goldens captured in software CI will not match hardware ANGLE.
findings.evidence: All measurements above are on ANGLE (Apple, ANGLE Metal Renderer: Apple M2 Max) — the top of the M-series range: 2.32 ms for the plain 1.18 M-triangle pass, 2.24 ms with wireframe, 2.07 ms with hardware clip planes, ~1.05 ms for 3-layer slice compositing. On a base M1/M2 (roughly a quarter of the M2 Max GPU) the same mesh pass lands near 8–10 ms, leaving nothing for slices, caps, and overlays inside an 8 ms budget. Extension availability was read from `gl.getSupportedExtensions()` on this machine only; nothing in the contract probes it at runtime.
findings.fix: (a) Add a startup GPU probe to §7.1 that records `UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL` and the set of missing extensions, shows a visible banner when the renderer is SwiftShader/llvmpipe, and selects a reduced-quality profile. (b) Declare the required-vs-optional extension list with a fallback for each. (c) Restate §9 against a named reference machine ("M1 Pro, 1440p, 2× DPR") and add the adaptive-quality rule from the previous finding so the target is a guarantee, not a hope. (d) Make Playwright goldens renderer-tagged with a tolerance, or run rendering CI on a GPU runner — SwiftShader goldens will not match ANGLE/Metal.

findings.title: §9's targets are written against files that do not exist, and omit the largest ones that do
findings.claim: The performance table benchmarks "T1.nii.gz 256³ int16" and "ernie.msh (5.9 M elements)" at "176 MB", but the real files are 256×256×208 and 184,207,351 bytes. More importantly the dataset's largest meshes — the 255 MB and 396 MB `*_TI.msh` files carrying the element fields that are the whole point of the "electric fields" requirement — have no target at all, and a 512×512×416 upsampled volume has none either.
findings.evidence: Header/`ls` from /Users/idohaber/datasets/000/derivatives/SimNIBS/sub-ernie: m2m_ernie/T1.nii.gz dims (256,256,208) dtype 4 (int16); m2m_ernie/ernie.msh 184,207,351 B; Simulations/Thalamus/TI/mesh/Thalamus_TI.msh 255,005,467 B; Simulations/flex_20260709_011433_.../TI/mesh/*_TI.msh 396,601,700 B; m2m_ernie/label_prep/*_upsampled.nii.gz 512×512×416.
findings.fix: Restate §9's rows against the actual file names and sizes, and add rows for: load a 255 MB element-field mesh to first frame with the field coloured; load a 396 MB mesh (or state it as explicitly out of scope for v1 with the reason); load and slice a 512×512×416 label volume. Fix §6.2's "176 MB" to 184 MB so the parse-throughput target means what it says.

reviews.verdict: The contract is unusually good for a v1 architecture doc — the data model, coordinate conventions, worker boundary with latest-wins scheduling, and exact-CPU-caps-plus-GPU-clipping split are all the right calls, and I verified that the headline raster target is real: 1.18 M de-indexed triangles with barycentric wireframe and 4×MSAA render in 2.24 ms at 2880×1620 on an M2 Max, so 60 fps orbit of ernie is comfortably achievable. The choice of raw WebGL2 over three.js/NiiVue is also vindicated by a fact the doc doesn't cite: ESSL 3.00 forbids dynamically-indexed sampler arrays, so the N-layer slice compositing this app needs is quad-per-layer no matter what engine hosts it. What will actually derail the build is the interactive geometry path, not the raster path: `plane_cut` is an unindexed full scan of 4.72 M tets (measured ~290 ms per scan) against a ≥30 fps drag target, `tag_surfaces` needlessly forces a 265 MB topology build on load when ernie.msh already ships its 1.18 M boundary triangles, the GPU format table has no filterable 16-bit path (174 ms to upload one 512³ volume as R32F), clipping is specified as `discard` when hardware clip distances are present and 28% faster, and "lagless" has no frame pump, no interaction-quality split, and no adaptive fallback behind it. Fix those five plus the oblique-slice model gap before Phase 1 starts and the rest is execution.

findings.title: wasm32's 4 GiB linear-memory ceiling is blown by files already in the reference dataset, and wasm memory can never shrink
findings.claim: The contract puts every parse and all topology in one long-lived wasm32 instance and sets a global bar of "memory < 1.5 GB", but never accounts for wasm32's hard 4 GiB cap or the fact that wasm linear memory only grows. Measured peaks for the very files listed in AGENTS.md exceed the stated budget, and `m2m_ernie/ernie_seeg.msh` — in the same subject directory — needs ~2.8 GB in a single load, leaving no room for a second dataset. Because there is no shrink, `free(handle)` returns memory to the Rust allocator, not to the OS, so the worker's high-water mark is permanent and a second large mesh lands on a fragmented 1.4 GB heap.
findings.evidence:
Measured on the real files (counts read out of the binaries, not estimated).

V8 limits, measured in node v25.4.0 (same V8 as Electron's Chromium): `new WebAssembly.Memory({initial:1,maximum:65536})` OK, `maximum:65537` → "value 65537 is above the upper bound 65536"; repeated `grow(1024)` failed at 64512 pages → **4032 MiB usable, not 4096**. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(WebAssembly.Memory.prototype)` = `['constructor','grow','buffer']` — **no shrink**.

`ernie.msh` (184,207,351 B; 847,165 nodes; 1,177,213 tri3; 4,722,625 tet4; **9,509,557 unique faces measured**, 128,614 boundary):
- input `&[u8]` param → malloc+memcpy into wasm: 184.2 MB
- retained Mesh (nodes 10.2 + tets 75.6 + tet_tags 18.9 + tris 14.1 + tri_tags 4.7 + gmsh_node_numbers 6.8): **130.3 MB**
- retained TetTopology (faces 9,509,557×12 = 114.1 + face_tets ×8 = 76.1 + tet_faces 4,722,625×16 = 75.6): **265.8 MB**
- sort transient: 18,890,500 face instances × (u64 key 8 + u32 payload 4) × 2 for radix ping-pong = **453.5 MB**
→ **peak ≈ 1,034 MB** before Vec-growth slack.

`Simulations/L_Insula/high_Frequency/mesh/ernie_TDCS_1_scalar.msh` (420 MB, E vec3 + magnE): 420.2 + 130.3 + 94.4 (fields as f32) + 265.8 + 453.5 = **1,364 MB** — already over the §9 bar for one file.

`m2m_ernie/ernie_seeg.msh` (492,090,201 B; 2,301,899 nodes; 2,612,423 tri3; **13,033,527 tet4**; 52,134,108 face instances, ~26.1 M unique): 492 (input) + 348 (mesh) + 730 (topology) + 1,251 (radix transient) = **~2,821 MB peak**, i.e. 70 % of the 4032 MB ceiling for one file, with no headroom for a T1 volume, a second sim mesh, or allocator fragmentation.

512³ f32 volume: 536,870,912 B of data. `read_nifti(bytes)->Volume` owns a Vec (512 MiB) + input bytes (512 MiB uncompressed, or inflate output) + `gpu_payload()` returning a second owned buffer (512 MiB) = **~1.5 GiB wasm peak for one volume**; then wasm-bindgen copies 512 MiB to JS, the UI keeps `data: TypedArray` (§4) = 512 MiB, the worker "keeps a copy" for marching cubes (§5) = 512 MiB, and the R32F 3D texture = 512 MiB VRAM → **~2.0 GB resident for one volume**.
findings.fix:
Four changes, all needed:
1. **Worker (and wasm instance) per large dataset, terminated on close.** Terminating a Worker is the only way to return linear memory to the OS. Replace "a dedicated Web Worker … owns parsed datasets by handle" in §5 with a pool: one long-lived worker for cheap ops, plus one disposable worker per mesh > 100 MB. `free(handle)` becomes `worker.terminate()`.
2. **Never copy the file into wasm.** Stream-parse: expose `parse_msh_chunk(&js_sys::Uint8Array)` fed from a `fetch()` ReadableStream, or (simpler) have the worker hold the bytes in JS and expose `read_at(offset,len)` — either way drop the 184–492 MB `&[u8]` malloc. That alone is 12–17 % of the ceiling.
3. **Replace the u64-key radix with a counting sort keyed on the face's minimum vertex.** Bucket the 4·T face instances by `min(v)` using a `Vec<u32>` of `n_nodes+1` counts (2.3 M nodes → 9.2 MB), then sort within buckets on the remaining two u32s. Transient drops from 453 MB → ~227 MB for ernie and 1,251 MB → ~626 MB for ernie_seeg, it stays deterministic, and it removes the packed-key width limit entirely (see the separate 21-bit finding).
4. **Drop `tet_faces` from `TetTopology`** (75.6 MB / 208 MB) — nothing in §6.3/§6.4 consumes it; `boundary_faces` and `plane_cut` only need `faces` + `face_tets`. Add `pub fn wasm_heap_bytes() -> u32` to §6.4 so §9's memory bar is measurable rather than asserted.

findings.title: wasm-pack `--target web` init calls `fetch()`, which Chromium refuses under Electron's `file://` — the Phase-0 gate cannot pass as written
findings.claim: ROADMAP Phase 0 pins `scripts/build-wasm.sh` to `wasm-pack --target web` and gates on "Electron window shows a WebGL2 triangle whose colour came from a WASM call". The generated `--target web` glue loads the module with `fetch(new URL('*_bg.wasm', import.meta.url))`. In a packaged Electron app the renderer is loaded with `loadFile()` → `file://` origin, and Chromium blocks `fetch()`/XHR on `file://` URLs. Additionally `WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming` requires `Content-Type: application/wasm`, which neither `file://` nor a naive custom protocol supplies. This works in `pnpm dev` (Vite http://localhost) and fails only in the packaged build — i.e. it will be discovered in Phase 3, not Phase 0.
findings.evidence:
Built the exact toolchain on this machine: rustc 1.93.0, wasm-pack 0.15.0, wasm-bindgen 0.2.127. `wasm-pack build --target web --release` succeeded; the generated `pkg/wtest.js` contains verbatim:
```js
if (module_or_path === undefined) { module_or_path = new URL('wtest_bg.wasm', import.meta.url); }
…
if (typeof module_or_path === 'string' || … module_or_path instanceof URL) { module_or_path = fetch(module_or_path); }
```
and the streaming path warns "`WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming` failed because your server does not serve Wasm with `application/wasm` MIME type". Electron docs confirm the working alternative: `protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged` with `{standard: true, secure: true, supportFetchAPI: true}` makes a scheme "adhere to RFC 3986 generic URI syntax" and enables the fetch API, and `protocol.handle(scheme, handler)` returns a `Response` whose headers you control.
findings.fix:
Make the privileged-scheme decision part of the contract, in §5 and Phase 0:

- In Electron main: `protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged([{ scheme: 'tetravox', privileges: { standard: true, secure: true, supportFetchAPI: true, stream: true, corsEnabled: true } }])` and `protocol.handle('tetravox', …)` serving the renderer bundle, `*_bg.wasm` with `content-type: application/wasm`, **and** the user's data files (see the IPC finding).
- Load the window with `win.loadURL('tetravox://app/index.html')`, never `loadFile()`.
- Phase 0's gate must be "the packaged `.dmg`/`.AppImage` shows the WASM-coloured triangle", not the dev server, so this is caught on day one.
- Belt and braces: also support `initSync({ module: <ArrayBuffer> })` so the worker can be handed pre-read bytes.

findings.title: §6.4's "returns views into WASM memory" is unsound — `memory.grow` detaches every outstanding view — and it also misdescribes what wasm-bindgen actually generates
findings.claim: §6.4 says "Each call returns views into WASM memory; the TS worker glue copies into transferable buffers", and §5 repeats "copied out of WASM memory into fresh ArrayBuffers and transferred". Two problems. (a) Any `Uint8Array` view onto `wasm.memory.buffer` is silently zero-lengthed the instant a later allocation triggers `memory.grow` — and `load_mesh` is specified to return **five** arrays (`nodes, tets, tris, tags, …`) at once, so the first views are dead by the time the last is produced if each is a separate allocation. (b) For the idiomatic `Vec<T>` return, wasm-bindgen already produces a fresh, transferable ArrayBuffer; a second copy in the worker glue is pure waste (an extra 114 MB copy and 114 MB peak for ernie's face array). The contract as written prescribes either an unsound pattern or a redundant one.
findings.evidence:
Detachment, node v25.4.0: `const m=new WebAssembly.Memory({initial:1}); const v=new Uint8Array(m.buffer); m.grow(1);` → `v.byteLength === 0`, `v.buffer.detached === true`. wasm-bindgen guards only its *own* cached views (`if (cached… === null || cached….byteLength === 0) cached… = new Uint32Array(wasm.memory.buffer)`), not anything the caller holds.

I compiled three signatures with wasm-bindgen 0.2.127 and read the emitted glue:
- `pub fn make(n) -> Vec<u32>` → `getArrayU32FromWasm0(ret[0],ret[1]).slice(); wasm.__wbindgen_free(...)` — **one** copy, into a fresh transferable ArrayBuffer. Already done for you.
- `pub fn fill(out: &mut [MaybeUninit<u32>])` → `passArray32ToWasm0(out, wasm.__wbindgen_malloc)` (copies JS→wasm, even for MaybeUninit) then an import callback `arg0.set(getArrayU32FromWasm0(...))` (copies wasm→JS): **two** copies plus a full-size wasm malloc. The "caller-provided buffer" idea is strictly the worst option here.
- `pub fn fill_into(dst: &js_sys::Uint32Array, n)` calling `dst.copy_from(&v)` → a single `arg0.set(getArrayU32FromWasm0(arg1,arg2))`: **one** memcpy, straight into a JS-owned, already-transferable buffer, with no wasm-side output buffer needing to survive the call.
findings.fix:
Replace the §6.4 paragraph with an explicit rule:

> Bulk results are returned either as `Vec<T>` (wasm-bindgen already `.slice()`s into a fresh transferable ArrayBuffer — the worker transfers `result.buffer` **as-is**, no second copy) or, for hot-path recycled buffers, by passing a `&js_sys::Float32Array`/`&js_sys::Uint32Array` the worker owns and writing with `copy_from` (one memcpy, no wasm-side output allocation). **Never** hand a `js_sys::*Array::view()` onto `wasm.memory.buffer` across a wasm call boundary, and never use `&mut [MaybeUninit<T>]` for outputs — it costs two copies.

And add the hot-path consequence: for `mesh_cut` at ≥30 fps the worker must keep a **pool** of recycled ArrayBuffers, transferring them back from the UI thread after upload (transfer moves ownership, so the UI thread must return them). Add `mesh_cut(handle, plane, maskId, out: {positions, ownerTet, tag, …})` taking the pooled arrays and returning only the element counts.

findings.title: The packed 3×21-bit face key overflows on a mesh in the reference dataset (2,301,899 nodes = 22 bits)
findings.claim: "build_topology … sort-based (radix on packed keys)" implies the canonical face `(v0<v1<v2)` is packed into one u64. Three vertex indices fit a u64 only at ≤21 bits each (2,097,152 nodes). `m2m_ernie/ernie_seeg.msh` — sitting in the same `m2m_ernie/` directory the contract names as test data — has 2,301,899 nodes, needing 22 bits. A 21-bit packing silently aliases distinct faces onto the same key, producing a corrupt topology (wrong boundary, wrong caps) with **no error** — the worst possible failure mode for a viewer, and one that golden tests on ernie.msh (847,165 nodes, 20 bits) will never catch.
findings.evidence: Read directly from the file headers: `m2m_ernie/ernie.msh` → 847,165 nodes (`(n-1).bit_length()` = 20); `m2m_ernie/ernie_seeg.msh` → 2,301,899 nodes (22 bits), 15,645,950 elements (2,612,423 tri3 + 13,033,527 tet4). 3 × 22 = 66 > 64.
findings.fix: State the bound and pick a scheme that has none. Preferred (also fixes the memory finding): counting-sort by `v0 = min(a,b,c)` into `n_nodes` buckets using a `Vec<u32>` prefix-sum array, then sort each bucket on `(v1, v2)` as a plain `u64` pair — no packing, no width limit, O(n), deterministic. If a packed key is kept, add to §6.3: "`build_topology` returns `Error::Unsupported` when `n_nodes >= 2^21`" **and** a synthetic fixture with ≥ 2^21 nodes in the Phase-1 test set, plus a real-data test on `ernie_seeg.msh`.

findings.title: §6.2 does not state that Gmsh v2 binary node coords and $NodeData/$ElementData values are float64 with an int32 id column, and its "file element order" assumption is not guaranteed by the format
findings.claim: §6.2 gives `Field { data: Vec<f32> }` and says "`$ElementData` is given in file element order (SimNIBS writes tris first, then tets) → split into per-kind vectors", with no mention of the on-disk representation. In Gmsh 2.2 binary with data-size 8, node coordinates are **float64** and every `$NodeData`/`$ElementData` record is `int32 id` followed by `ncomp × float64`. So (a) every field needs an f64→f32 narrowing pass the contract never mentions, (b) the record is **not** a packed array — the interleaved id column means you cannot `bytemuck::cast_slice` the region, and (c) the data is addressed **by element id**, not by position; Gmsh permits partial fields (`nr < n_elements`) and arbitrary id order. "File element order" happens to hold for SimNIBS output but silently corrupts any field written by Gmsh itself or by a cropping tool.
findings.evidence: Parsed the real binaries. `ernie.msh` header is `2.2 1 8`; `$Nodes` records unpack as `dtype([('id','<i4'),('coord','<f8',3)])` (28 B/node, id 1..847165 contiguous). `Thalamus_TI.msh`: one `$ElementData` `"TI_max"`, string-tags=1, real-tags=1, **integer-tags=4** `[0, 1, 5899838, 0]`, ncomp=1, records = `int32 id + float64` (12 B × 5,899,838 = 70.8 MB, which is exactly the 255,005,467 − 184,207,351 = 70.8 MB difference from `ernie.msh`). `ernie_TDCS_1_scalar.msh` has `"E"` with integer-tags `[0, 3, 5900498, 0]` (ncomp=3 → 28 B/record) and `"magnE"` (ncomp=1). SimNIBS's own reader (`mesh_io.py` `read_ElementData`) reads exactly `dtype([('id',np.int32),('values',np.float64,nr_comp)])` and then *raises* if `np.any(elm_number != m.elm.elm_number)` — i.e. it does not support out-of-order or partial data either; that is SimNIBS's limitation, not the format's.
findings.fix:
Add to §6.2:

> Gmsh v2 binary with `data-size 8`: `$Nodes` records are `i32 id + 3×f64`; `$NodeData`/`$ElementData` records are `i32 id + ncomp×f64`. Values are narrowed to `f32` on read (document the precision loss); the id column forbids a zero-copy cast, so read with a strided loop. **Scatter by id** into a pre-sized `Vec<f32>` rather than assuming positional order; when `nr < n_elements`, fill the gaps with `f32::NAN` and set `Field.partial = true` so the shader can `discard`. Header tag counts are variable — read `n_string_tags` / `n_real_tags` / `n_integer_tags` and skip the extras (SimNIBS writes 1 / 1 / 4; Gmsh may write 2 string tags for an interpolation scheme). `ncomp` comes from `integer_tags[1]`, `nr` from `integer_tags[2]`; `integer_tags[0]` is the time-step index (>1 step ⇒ 4-D field, currently `Unsupported`).

Also fix the element-block skip arithmetic for unsupported types: the block header is `(elm_type, count, n_tags)` and the skip is `count × (1 + n_tags + nodes_per_type) × 4` bytes — SimNIBS's own code has this wrong (`nr * (3 + nr_nodes_elm[elm_type])`, hard-coding 2 tags into a 3), so do not copy it.

findings.title: §4/§7.3 promise trilinear scalar volumes but the format list contains no WebGL2-filterable format for the data actually on disk
findings.claim: §4 fixes `gpu.format: 'R8'|'R16UI'|'R32F'|'RGBA8'` and §7.3 says "`sampler3D` (trilinear) for scalars". In WebGL2 core, **R32F is not texture-filterable** — binding it with `LINEAR` makes the texture incomplete and every sample returns black. `R16UI` is an integer format and is NEAREST-only by definition. So of the four listed formats only `R8` and `RGBA8` can be trilinearly filtered, and the reference dataset's T1 is float32. There is also no filterable 16-bit path: WebGL2 core has no normalized `R16` (that is the `EXT_texture_norm16` extension), so int16/uint16 MRI has nowhere to go either. This is a black-screen-on-real-data defect, not a quality nit.
findings.evidence:
MDN's WebGL2 sized-internal-format table: `R16F | RED | HALF_FLOAT, FLOAT | Color renderable: Y | Texture filterable: Y`; `R32F | RED | FLOAT` has **neither** column marked. `OES_texture_float_linear` is what makes R32F/RG32F/RGBA32F filterable and it remains an *extension* in WebGL2 (Firefox bug 1330433 exists precisely because "OES_texture_float_linear + WebGL2 should make R32F and RG32F filterable" was not implemented); `OES_texture_half_float_linear`'s functionality, by contrast, is core in WebGL2.

The data contradicts the plan's assumption too: `m2m_ernie/T1.nii.gz` is **datatype 16 = FLOAT32**, dim `256×256×208` (54.5 MB as f32) — not the "256³ int16" claimed in §9 and AGENTS.md. `final_tissues.nii.gz` is datatype 512 = UINT16. All the `Simulations/Thalamus/TI/niftis/*.nii.gz` E-field maps are datatype 16 (float32).
findings.fix: Change the §4 format union to `'R8'|'R16F'|'R16UI'|'R32F'|'RGBA8'` and make **R16F the default for all scalar volumes** (float32 and 16-bit integer alike; half-float carries 11 bits of mantissa — exact for 0..2047 and ample for MRI intensity, E-fields and t-maps after the window transform). Add to §7.3: "`R32F` is used only when `gl.getExtension('OES_texture_float_linear')` is non-null **or** `interpolation === 'nearest'`; the engine probes at context creation and records the fallback in `VolumeDataset.gpu`." Halving to R16F also halves the 512³ budget (512 MB → 256 MB VRAM), which the memory finding needs.

findings.title: NIfTI qfac (`pixdim[0]`) is unmentioned, and it is −1 in every volume of the reference dataset
findings.claim: §3's rule is "NIfTI sform if `sform_code>0`, else qform if `qform_code>0`, else `diag(pixdim)`" and §6.1 lists the quaternion fields implicitly under "affine". The single most-missed NIfTI-1 detail is absent: the qform rotation's **third column must be multiplied by `qfac = (pixdim[0] < 0 ? -1 : 1)`**. Omitting it produces a left–right (or A–P) mirrored volume — a silent, clinically dangerous error in a viewer whose §3 also promises a neurological/radiological convention. The `diag(pixdim)` fallback is also wrong in a second way: `pixdim[0]` is qfac, not a spacing, so the fallback must be `diag(pixdim[1..4])`.
