findings.evidence: Read the raw headers of the reference data: `m2m_ernie/T1.nii.gz`, `final_tissues.nii.gz`, `segmentation/labeling.nii.gz` and all `Simulations/Thalamus/TI/niftis/*.nii.gz` have `pixdim = (-1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)` — **qfac = −1 in every one**. Their affines are also non-diagonal permutations (`srow_x = (0,0,1,−99.737)`, `srow_y = (−1,0,0,154.188)`, `srow_z = (0,1,0,−143.642)`), so the `diag(pixdim)` fallback would be catastrophically wrong for any sibling file lacking both codes. `labeling.nii.gz` has `qform_code = sform_code = 1` while the others have 2 — both branches are live in this dataset.
findings.fix: Rewrite the §3 bullet as: "Source: NIfTI `sform` if `sform_code > 0`; else the qform built from `(quatern_b,c,d)` with `a = sqrt(1 − b² − c² − d²)`, translation `(qoffset_x,y,z)`, scaling `pixdim[1..3]`, and **`qfac = pixdim[0] < 0 ? −1 : +1` applied to the third column**; else `diag(pixdim[1], pixdim[2], pixdim[3], 1)`." Add a real-data test asserting the world coordinate of voxel `(0,0,0)` and `(255,255,207)` of `m2m_ernie/T1.nii.gz` against nibabel, and a synthetic fixture with `sform_code = 0, qform_code = 1, pixdim[0] = −1` — the only case that catches a missing qfac.

findings.title: §6.4 omits `build_topology`, cancellation, and progress — the first cut-plane drag will freeze for ~1.5 s and latest-wins cannot prevent it
findings.claim: §6.3 exposes `build_topology` but §6.4's worker API has no entry for it, so the TS side can only trigger it implicitly as a side effect of the first `mesh_cut`/`mesh_boundary`. That first call therefore costs ~1–1.5 s plus an ~850 MB allocation spike, inside a code path §9 budgets at ≥30 fps. Worse, the "latest-wins" design in §5 is described as if it prevents stalls — it doesn't: **a wasm call cannot be interrupted**. Latest-wins bounds the *queue* to one entry, but the in-flight call still runs to completion; the only way to abort is `worker.terminate()`. There is also no progress channel anywhere, so a 3 s ernie parse and a 1.5 s topology build both present as a frozen UI.
findings.evidence: Measured: numpy's introsort over the 18,890,500 packed u64 face keys of ernie.msh (`np.unique` with counts) takes 1.07 s natively on this M-series machine, on a highly-tuned native sort. A hand-written wasm32 single-threaded radix over the same data will not beat that; 1–1.5 s in wasm is the honest number, which is what §6.3 itself claims ("ernie < 1.5 s WASM"). The allocation spike is derived in the memory finding (~849 MB excluding the input buffer).
findings.fix: Add to §6.4: `mesh_build_topology(handle) -> Promise<{faces: number, boundary: number}>` as an explicit, awaitable step, called eagerly right after `load_mesh` with a progress bar — never lazily from a drag frame. Add `progress(requestId, phase, done, total)` as a worker→client message, emitted from a `&js_sys::Function` callback threaded through the long parsers. And correct §5's claim to: "latest-wins drops *queued* stale requests; an in-flight wasm call runs to completion. Ops that can exceed one frame (`load_*`, `build_topology`, `marching_*`) run on a disposable worker so they can be aborted by `terminate()`; only sub-frame ops (`mesh_cut`, `mesh_isolate`) run on the resident worker."

findings.title: rayon in the compute worker requires nightly Rust *and* cross-origin isolation, which `loadFile()` can never provide — Phase 3's "rayon in WASM if needed" is not a drop-in
findings.claim: §5 says the worker is "single-threaded v1; rayon-ready" and Phase 3 lists "rayon in WASM if needed" as a tuning knob. It is not a knob — it changes the toolchain, the build target, the shell configuration, and the crate-purity constraint. wasm threads need `SharedArrayBuffer`, which needs `crossOriginIsolated`, which needs COOP `same-origin` + COEP `require-corp` response headers on the top-level document; an Electron window loaded with `loadFile()` sits on a `file://` opaque origin that can never be cross-origin isolated. Separately, `-C target-feature=+atomics,+bulk-memory` requires rebuilding std via `-Zbuild-std`, which is still **nightly-only** — directly contradicting §1's implicit stable-Rust posture and §10's `clippy -D warnings` CI. Deciding this in Phase 3 means retrofitting shell + build + CI after the code exists.
findings.evidence: Chrome 92+ requires cross-origin isolation for SharedArrayBuffer (`WorkerGlobalScope.crossOriginIsolated`); COOP/COEP are response headers and cannot be set via `<meta http-equiv>`. wasm-bindgen-rayon's own requirements as of 2026: a nightly toolchain with `rust-src`, `rustflags = ["-C","target-feature=+atomics,+bulk-memory"]`, and `[unstable] build-std = ["panic_abort","std"]` — "Cargo's `-Zbuild-std` … remains a requirement because wasm threads have not yet been stabilized". Also note §6.3's "Determinism: same input → byte-identical output (needed for golden tests)" is broken by any rayon float reduction (`stats()` mean, field min/max) unless the chunking is fixed and order-independent.
findings.fix:
Decide now, in §5 and DECISIONS.md, one of:
(a) **Single-threaded, permanently.** Delete "rayon-ready" and the Phase-3 bullet; get parallelism instead by running independent datasets in separate workers (which you already need for the memory finding). This is the recommendation — it is free and it composes with worker-per-dataset.
(b) **Threads.** Then Phase 0 must already ship: the privileged `tetravox://` scheme with `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` and `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` on the document response (`protocol.handle` returns a `Response`, so this is one header object), a pinned nightly in `rust-toolchain.toml`, `-Zbuild-std` in CI on both macOS and Ubuntu, and an assertion `self.crossOriginIsolated === true` in the worker.
Either way add to §6.3: "parallel reductions use fixed-size chunks with a deterministic tree merge, so results are bit-identical to the serial path."

findings.title: The main→renderer→worker file path costs three full copies and the diagram's "(transfer)" annotation is wrong for cross-process IPC
findings.claim: §5's diagram shows `ipc: openFile(path) → ArrayBuffer (transfer)` from Electron main to the renderer. Transferables do not cross process boundaries — Electron IPC serializes with the V8 structured-clone serializer over Mojo and **copies** the ArrayBuffer; only `MessagePort` objects are transferable via `ipcRenderer.postMessage`. So a 492 MB `ernie_seeg.msh` is: Node `readFile` buffer (492 MB in main) → serialize → deserialize in the renderer (492 MB) → `postMessage` transfer to the worker (free) → wasm-bindgen `&[u8]` malloc+memcpy (492 MB in wasm) = three resident copies with a main-process peak the contract never budgets, plus main-process gunzip which must fully materialize the output before the first byte is sent.
findings.evidence: Electron's `protocol` docs confirm the alternative is first-class: `registerSchemesAsPrivileged` with `supportFetchAPI: true` "supports fetch API, streaming video/audio", and `protocol.handle(scheme, handler)` returns a `Response` — i.e. a `ReadableStream` body. File sizes in the reference dataset that make this matter: `ernie_seeg.msh` 492,090,201 B, `ernie_tes_flex_opt_head_mesh.msh` 467,399,832 B, several `ernie_TDCS_*_scalar.msh` at 420 MB, `Thalamus_TI.msh` 255,005,467 B.
findings.fix: Delete the bulk-bytes IPC path. Keep IPC for the *dialog* only (`openFile() → path`), then have the **worker** stream the bytes itself: `fetch('tetravox://file/' + encodeURIComponent(path))` served by the same `protocol.handle` you need for the wasm module, with `Content-Encoding` handled by Chromium so `.nii.gz` is inflated by the network stack (native, streaming, zero main-process buffering) — that also lets you drop `miniz_oxide` from the hot path while keeping it for the plain-browser build §5 wants. Update the §5 diagram to `ipc: openFile() → path` and add: "Bulk bytes never traverse IPC. Electron IPC copies ArrayBuffers; only MessagePorts transfer across processes."

findings.title: `scl_slope` → F32 widening contradicts `GpuPayload {scale, offset}` and doubles volume memory for no benefit
findings.claim: §6.1's rule "apply `scl_slope/scl_inter` when slope ∉ {0,1} or inter ≠ 0 → F32" converts an int16 volume to f32 in wasm (2× memory), on the UI heap (2×), and in VRAM (2×) — and then lands on R32F, which is the format that isn't filterable. Meanwhile the same section's `GpuPayload { format, bytes, scale, offset }` already carries exactly the two numbers needed to do the affine in the shader for free. The two rules contradict each other, and §4's `dtype` comment ("on-disk type after scl_slope/inter folding rules") locks the wasteful one into the data model.
findings.evidence: §6.1 and §4 as written. Cost on real data: a 256×256×208 int16 volume is 27.3 MB native and 54.5 MB as f32; for a 512³ volume it is 256 MB vs 512 MB, in three places each.
findings.fix: Invert the rule: "`scl_slope`/`scl_inter` are **not** folded into the samples. The native dtype is preserved and the affine is carried in `GpuPayload{scale, offset}` and applied in the fragment shader (`value = raw*scale + offset`) and in the CPU probe path. Widening to F32 happens only for `float64` input and for `RGB24`→`RGBA8`." Then `VolumeDataset.stats` must state whether it is in raw or physical units — make it physical (post-scale), since window/threshold in §7.3 are user-facing physical values.

findings.title: Mask lifetime, cut-vertex interpolation type, and cap normals are underspecified in a way that blocks the TS engine
findings.claim: Three concrete API gaps an engine implementer hits on day one. (a) `mesh_isolate(handle, criteriaJSON) -> maskId` allocates a `BitMask` in wasm with no `free_mask(maskId)` and no stated lifetime — every isolation edit leaks 590 KB for ernie, 1.6 MB for ernie_seeg, and the leak is invisible because the handle table hides it. (b) `Cut { … bary_node: Vec<[u32;2]>+t … }` is not a type; a cut vertex lies on a tet edge, so the interpolation record is `(n0, n1, t)` per **vertex** (3 per de-indexed triangle), and the contract never says the count or whether `t` is a separate `Vec<f32>`. (c) `Cut` has no normals, but §7.4's mesh shader requires a `normal` attribute; cap normals are constant (the plane normal) and the engine can synthesize them, but only if the contract says so — otherwise every agent invents a different answer.
findings.evidence: Read from §6.3/§6.4 directly. Sizes: `BitMask(Vec<u64>)` over 4,722,625 tets = 590,336 B; over `ernie_seeg.msh`'s 13,033,527 tets = 1,629,192 B.
findings.fix: In §6.4 add `mesh_free_mask(handle, maskId)` and state "masks are owned by the mesh handle and released with it; the client frees eagerly on every isolation change." In §6.3 make the type explicit: `pub struct Cut { positions: Vec<f32> /*3/vertex*/, bary_edge: Vec<[u32;2]> /*1/vertex*/, bary_t: Vec<f32> /*1/vertex*/, owner_tet: Vec<u32> /*1/tri*/, tag: Vec<i32> /*1/tri*/, edge_segments: Vec<f32>, boundary_segments: Vec<f32> }` and add one line to §7.4: "cap normals are the (negated) clip-plane normal, generated engine-side; `Cut` carries no normal buffer."

findings.title: GIfTI's actual on-disk encoding (`GZipBase64Binary`) and its variants are absent from the format contract
findings.claim: §6.2 specifies `read_gifti` as "(pointset+triangle, transforms)" with no mention of encodings. GIfTI `DataArray` has four legal `Encoding` values — `ASCII`, `Base64Binary`, `GZipBase64Binary`, `ExternalFileBinary` — plus an `Endian` attribute and an `ArrayIndexingOrder` of `RowMajorOrder` or `ColumnMajorOrder`. The reference surfaces use the one that needs both a base64 decoder and an inflate, and `ExternalFileBinary` (used by HCP-style `.gii` + sidecar) cannot be served at all by a `read_gifti(bytes)` signature that has no access to the sibling file.
findings.evidence: Read the header of `m2m_ernie/surfaces/lh.pial.gii`: `<DataArray Intent="NIFTI_INTENT_POINTSET" DataType="NIFTI_TYPE_FLOAT32" ArrayIndexingOrder="RowMajorOrder" Dimensionality="2" Encoding="GZipBase64Binary" Endian="LittleEndian" ExternalFileName="" ExternalFileOffset="0" Dim0="245762" Dim1="3">`, with a `<CoordinateSystemTransformMatrix>` whose `DataSpace` is `NIFTI_XFORM_UNKNOWN` and `TransformedSpace` is `NIFTI_XFORM_SCANNER_ANAT` (identity here, but the pair must be honoured in general).
findings.fix: Expand the §6.2 line: "`read_gifti` handles `Encoding` ∈ {ASCII, Base64Binary, GZipBase64Binary}; `ExternalFileBinary` returns `Error::Unsupported` in v1 (the byte-slice signature has no sibling-file access). Honours `Endian`, `ArrayIndexingOrder` (Row/ColumnMajor), and applies `CoordinateSystemTransformMatrix` when `TransformedSpace == NIFTI_XFORM_SCANNER_ANAT`, recording `DataSpace`/`TransformedSpace` in the dataset so the UI can show it. `.func/.shape/.label.gii` become node `Field`s keyed by `Intent`; `<LabelTable>` becomes a `LabelLut`." Same treatment for `read_fs_surface`: state that the 3-byte magic is `0xFFFFFE` **big-endian** for triangle files, coordinates are big-endian f32, and the file is in tkr-RAS with the `cras` offset in the trailing `valid`/`filename` metadata block.

findings.title: `read_nifti(bytes: &[u8])` cannot represent a `.hdr`/`.img` pair, which the user's "a variety of nifti" explicitly covers
findings.claim: The single-byte-slice signature makes two-file NIfTI-1 (`magic == "ni1\0"`, 348-byte header in `.hdr`, voxels in `.img`, optionally each gzipped independently) unrepresentable. §6.1's prose says ".nii and .nii.gz" — so this is a scoping decision, but it is one the contract makes silently, and ANALYZE/`.hdr`+`.img` pairs are still common in older atlases and FSL-era outputs.
findings.evidence: §6.1's signature and prose. The magic distinction is in the NIfTI-1 header itself: offset 344 holds `"n+1\0"` for single-file and `"ni1\0"` for the paired form; my probe confirms the reference volumes are all `n+1\0` single-file, so nothing in the test set exercises the paired path.
findings.fix: Either add `pub fn read_nifti_pair(hdr: &[u8], img: &[u8]) -> Result<Volume>` and have the loader detect the `.hdr` extension and fetch the sibling, or add an explicit line to §6.1: "`ni1` (two-file `.hdr`/`.img`) returns `Error::Unsupported(\"two-file NIfTI\")` in v1" — so the failure is a clear message rather than a confusing parse error on a 348-byte file. Also widen the reject list note: NIfTI datatypes 1024/1280 (int64/uint64) appear in some label volumes; reject them by name, not by falling through.

findings.title: Determinism is asserted globally but two specified behaviours break it
findings.claim: §6.3 states "Determinism: same input → byte-identical output (needed for golden tests)", and §9 cross-checks parsers against reference values. Two specified things violate it: (a) §6.1 permits a "sampled histogram" for percentiles — sampling is non-deterministic unless the stride/seed is fixed and part of the contract; (b) golden tests that compare a native `cargo test` run against the wasm build will diverge for any transcendental, because wasm gets `libm`/compiler-builtins while native gets the platform libm (`sin`, `exp`, `pow` are not correctly rounded and differ across platforms). `sqrt` and the four arithmetic ops *are* correctly rounded and identical, so normals, lerps and marching cubes are safe — but nothing says so.
findings.evidence: §6.1's "(sampled histogram OK)" and §6.3's determinism sentence, read together. IEEE-754 guarantees correct rounding for `+ - * / sqrt` only; `libm` transcendentals are implementation-defined.
findings.fix: Tighten to: "Geometry outputs are byte-identical across native and wasm builds; they use only `+ - * / sqrt` and integer ops. Any use of a transcendental (`sin/cos/exp/pow`) makes a function native-vs-wasm-divergent and must be marked `#[doc(hidden)] // non-portable` and excluded from cross-build golden tests." And change §6.1 to "percentiles from a full 65536-bin histogram over `[min,max]` (exact for integer dtypes, ≤ 1/65536 relative error for float); the 256-bin display histogram is derived from it." That is one O(n) pass, deterministic, and removes the sampling question entirely.

findings.title: Test-data facts in §9 and AGENTS.md are wrong in ways that will mislead the parser and engine agents
findings.claim: Three stated facts about the reference data are wrong, and each one points an implementer at the wrong code path: T1 is described as int16 256³ (it is float32, 256×256×208), `Thalamus_TI.msh` is described as carrying "element fields incl. `TI_max`, vector `E`" (it carries only `TI_max`; the vector `E` lives in the `*_TDCS_*_scalar.msh` files), and the ernie tri tags are listed as "1001–1010" (the file also contains tag 1099, and the simulation meshes add 1101/1102/1501/1502/2101/2102 for electrode and gel surfaces plus tet tags 101/102/501/502).
findings.evidence: Header of `m2m_ernie/T1.nii.gz`: `datatype 16` (FLOAT32), `bitpix 32`, `dim = (3, 256, 256, 208, …)` → 13,631,488 voxels, 54.5 MB as f32. `Thalamus_TI.msh`: exactly one `$ElementData`, `"TI_max"`, ncomp 1; file size 255,005,467 = 184,207,351 (mesh) + 70,798,116 (one scalar f64 field with id column). `ernie.msh` tri tag1 values: {1001,1002,1003,1005,1006,1007,1008,1009,1010,**1099**}; tet tag1: {1,2,3,5,6,7,8,9,10} — note **4 is absent** in both. `ernie_TDCS_1_scalar.msh` tri tags add {1101,1102,1501,1502,2101,2102} and tet tags add {101,102,501,502}, and it carries `E` (ncomp 3) + `magnE` (ncomp 1).
findings.fix: Correct §9's first row to "Load `m2m_ernie/T1.nii.gz` (float32, 256×256×208, 54.5 MB decompressed) < 400 ms to first frame" and the AGENTS.md test-data block to match. Add the electrode/gel tag ranges to the §7.6 default-LUT discussion — a viewer that colours only 1–10 / 1001–1010 will render electrodes as untagged grey on every simulation mesh, which is the most common thing a SimNIBS user opens. Do not assume tags are contiguous; tag 4 is absent from ernie.

reviews.verdict: The rendering half of this contract is unusually well specified, but the Rust/WASM half rests on a memory model that the reference dataset breaks today: with one wasm instance owning all parsing and topology, `ernie.msh` peaks at ~1.03 GB, a 420 MB TDCS mesh at ~1.36 GB, and `m2m_ernie/ernie_seeg.msh` at ~2.8 GB against a measured 4032 MB V8 ceiling that never shrinks — so the second large file a user opens is an OOM, not a slowdown. Two more issues are hard stops rather than tuning: the packed 21-bit face key silently corrupts topology on the 2.3 M-node mesh in the same directory, and `wasm-pack --target web`'s `fetch()`-based init cannot load under Electron's `file://`, which means the Phase-0 gate as written can only be passed by the dev server. The fixes are all structural but cheap if made now — worker-per-dataset with `terminate()` as the free(), a privileged `tetravox://` scheme that carries the wasm module, the data files and (if threads are ever wanted) the COOP/COEP headers, a counting-sort topology with no key-width limit, and R16F as the default volume format since WebGL2 cannot trilinearly filter the R32F that the actual T1 requires; deferring any of them to Phase 3 means retrofitting the shell, the build and the data model after the code exists.

findings.title: Packaged Electron loads the renderer over file:// — fetch, instantiateStreaming and module Workers all fail there
findings.claim: The whole compute path — a module Web Worker that boots a wasm-pack `--target web` module — cannot start in a packaged build. electron-vite's production renderer is loaded with `loadFile()` (origin `null`, scheme `file:`). In that origin: `fetch('./x.wasm')` throws, `WebAssembly.instantiateStreaming` throws, and `new Worker('./compute-worker.js', {type:'module'})` throws outright. wasm-pack's generated `__wbg_init` defaults to `module_or_path = new URL('..._bg.wasm', import.meta.url)` followed by `fetch(module_or_path)` — i.e. exactly the failing call. This works in `pnpm dev` (vite dev server = http://localhost) and fails only in the packaged artefact, so it will be discovered at the Phase-3 packaging gate, after every agent has built against the broken assumption.
findings.evidence: Ran the real check under Playwright's Chromium (same engine as Electron 44) with the page loaded from a `file://` URL. Results: `fetchFile: "THREW: Failed to fetch"` (console: `Fetch API cannot load file:///…/m.wasm. URL scheme "file" is not supported.`), `instantiateStreaming: "THREW: Failed to fetch"`, `moduleWorker: "THREW: Failed to construct 'Worker': Script at 'file:///…/worker.mjs' cannot be accessed from origin 'null'."`. Separately built a probe crate with the installed wasm-pack 0.15.0 / wasm-bindgen 0.2.127; generated `pkg/tvxprobe.js` line 112: `module_or_path = new URL('tvxprobe_bg.wasm', import.meta.url);` line 117: `module_or_path = fetch(module_or_path);`.
findings.fix: Settle this in Phase 0 and write it into §5. Two acceptable shapes, pick one: (a) register a custom standard scheme in main — `protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged([{scheme:'app', privileges:{standard:true, secure:true, supportFetchAPI:true, stream:true}}])` + `protocol.handle('app', …)` — and load the renderer as `app://tetravox/index.html`; this makes fetch, module workers and streaming compilation all work and is also the right home for streaming large files (see the file-open finding). (b) Keep `file://` and (i) instantiate wasm with `initSync({ module: bytes })` from bytes handed in over IPC, and (ii) build the worker as a *classic* worker from a Blob URL (`new Worker(URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([src])))`) — classic workers from a blob are allowed, module workers from `file://` are not. Option (a) is strongly preferred; add it to DECISIONS.md and make "packaged app opens a NIfTI" a Phase-0 smoke test, not a Phase-3 one.

findings.title: The worker message protocol does not exist in the contract — the two agents on either side of it will build incompatible glue
findings.claim: §6.4 specifies the *wasm-bindgen* surface (`mesh_cut(handle, plane, maskId?)`) but nothing about the message layer that ROADMAP Phase 1 hands to two different agents in parallel: the `packages/wasm` agent writes `compute-worker.ts`/`compute-client.ts`, the `packages/engine` agent consumes it. Undefined: the envelope shape, how `requestId` is carried, how "latest-wins" is keyed (§5 says "per (layer, op)" but layers are an engine concept the worker knows nothing about), how errors cross the boundary (Rust `Error` enum → what on the JS side?), whether there is progress reporting for a 3 s parse, what the transfer list contains for a multi-array result like `Cut`, and the lifecycle of `maskId` (created by `mesh_isolate`, consumed by `mesh_boundary`, never freed by anything in the listed API). Two agents will ship two protocols and Phase 1 ends in an integration rewrite.
findings.evidence: §6.4 lists only free functions and return types. §5 says "Every compute request carries a request id; the client keeps only the newest pending request per (layer, op)" — `layer` is a `LayerId` from §4, which is engine state; the worker API in §6.4 is keyed by mesh `handle`. `free(handle)` exists; there is no `free_mask(maskId)`. No `Error` mapping, no progress, no cancel message.
findings.fix: Add §6.5 "Worker protocol" and make a frozen `packages/protocol/src/index.ts` a Phase-0 deliverable, owned by nobody afterwards (changing it requires editing ARCHITECTURE.md). Minimum: `type Req = { id: number; key: string; op: 'loadVolume'|'loadMesh'|'tagSurfaces'|'boundary'|'cut'|'isolate'|'field'|'elmToNode'|'locate'|'marchingCubes'|'marchingTets'|'contours'|'free'|'freeMask'; args: … }`; `type Res = { id: number; ok: true; result: …; transfer: ArrayBuffer[] } | { id: number; ok: false; error: { kind: 'parse'|'unsupported'|'io'|'oom'|'panic'; message: string } } | { id: number; progress: number; stage: string }`. Latest-wins is keyed on the caller-supplied opaque `key: string` (engine passes `"${layerId}:cut"`), not on layer ids the worker understands. Mask lifecycle: `isolate` returns `{maskId, generation}`; the client owns it and must call `freeMask`; the worker drops all masks when its mesh handle is freed. Specify that a wasm `panic!` poisons the module and the client must recreate the worker.

findings.title: A 256×1 RGBA LUT cannot represent FreeSurfer / .annot label ids — the atlas requirement fails as specified
findings.claim: §7.3 says "window/threshold/colormap via a 256×1 RGBA LUT texture" and §7.6 says label LUTs include FreeSurferColorLUT.txt and .annot label tables. Label ids in those files are not in 0..255 and are not dense: FreeSurferColorLUT.txt has 1266 entries with ids up to 14175, and FreeSurfer `.annot` stores per-vertex values as packed RGB (`r | g<<8 | b<<16`), reaching 14,474,380 for the DK40 file in the test data. Indexing a 256-texel LUT by raw label value is impossible for both. It is also not fixable by widening to a 1-D texture: MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE is 8192 under the software renderer CI will use, less than 14175. Two agents will pick different workarounds (one remaps on the CPU, one widens the texture) and the label-outline shader in §7.3 — which compares raw sampled label ids at ±1 pixel — depends on which.
findings.evidence: `awk '$1 ~ /^[0-9]+$/ {print $1}' resources/atlas/FreeSurferColorLUT.txt | sort -n | tail -1` → 14175, 1266 entries. Parsed `m2m_ernie/segmentation/lh.ernie_DK40.annot`: 245762 vertices, 36 unique annotation values, min 0, max 14474380, colortable tag present. Measured in Playwright Chromium: MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE 8192 under ANGLE/SwiftShader (headless) vs 16384 under ANGLE/Metal on an M2 Max (headed); MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE 2048 on both.
findings.fix: Amend §7.3/§7.6: continuous colormaps use a 256×1 RGBA8 LUT; **label LUTs use a separate path** — at load time the reader builds a dense `uniqueLabels: Uint32Array` (already in the §4 `stats`) plus an `id → denseIndex` map, rewrites the volume texture to R16UI dense indices (cap 65535, error above that), and uploads a `N×1 RGBA8` palette. For `.annot`, remap packed-RGB annotation values to 0..N-1 via the embedded colortable at parse time and return the colortable as the palette — say so explicitly in §6.2's `read_fs_annot` signature (`-> (Field /* dense 0..N-1 */, LabelTable /* index → (name, rgba, originalId) */)`). Note that outline detection then compares dense indices, and that the info panel must map back to the original id for display.

findings.title: Exact caps are specified for up to 6 clip planes but the geometry API only cuts with one
findings.claim: §4 gives `clip: { planes: ClipPlane[]; caps: boolean }`, §7.4 says "up to 6 planes as vec4 uniforms" plus "Caps come from `plane_cut` geometry (exact per-element polygons)", but §6.3 declares `plane_cut(mesh, topo, plane: &Plane, mask) -> Cut` — a single plane. Capping a tet mesh against 6 half-spaces is not 6 independent single-plane cuts: the cap polygon on plane A must itself be clipped by planes B..F, and tets fully removed by B must not contribute to A's cap. The `tvx-geom` agent will implement the signature as written; the `engine` agent will call it once per enabled plane and get caps that bleed past the other planes. This is exactly the "cut-through and cross-section visualization" the user asked for, so it is not a corner case.
findings.evidence: Contract text only: §6.3 signature takes `plane: &Plane`; §7.4 and §4 both assume N planes with caps. `Cut` is described in a prose comment containing `bary_node:Vec<[u32;2]>+t`, which is not a valid Rust type — so even the single-plane return shape is not agreed between the crate and the engine.
findings.fix: Change §6.3 to `pub fn plane_cut(mesh, topo, planes: &[Plane], mask: &BitMask) -> Vec<Cut>` returning one `Cut` per plane, each already clipped by the other planes, and write out the exact struct: `pub struct Cut { pub plane: usize, pub positions: Vec<f32>, pub owner_tet: Vec<u32>, pub tag: Vec<i32>, pub interp: Vec<CutInterp>, pub edge_segments: Vec<f32>, pub boundary_segments: Vec<f32> }` with `pub struct CutInterp { pub n0: u32, pub n1: u32, pub t: f32 }` (one per emitted vertex, for node-field interpolation). Cap v1 at 6 planes in the type too. Add a synthetic fixture — one tet with known vertices, cut by two known planes — with the expected vertex list committed as the golden, so both agents test against the same numbers.

findings.title: The file-open byte path is drawn as a zero-copy IPC transfer, which Electron does not have; measured ceilings make the alternative fragile too
findings.claim: §5's diagram says `ipc: openFile(path) → ArrayBuffer (transfer)`. Electron IPC serialises with the Structured Clone Algorithm and does not transfer ArrayBuffers — `ipcRenderer.invoke` copies. For the real files in scope that means a 176 MB copy for `ernie.msh`, 255 MB for `Thalamus_TI.msh` and 492 MB for `ernie_seeg.msh`, landing on the UI thread (which §5 promises never blocks), then another postMessage hop into the worker. It also collides with a renderer-side ceiling: a single ArrayBuffer larger than ~1.5 GB fails to allocate in the renderer, while Node in main has no such limit — so main can read a file the renderer cannot hold.
findings.evidence: Electron docs: arguments to `ipcRenderer.invoke` are serialised with the Structured Clone Algorithm; the transfer list on `webContents.postMessage` takes MessagePorts, not ArrayBuffers. Measured in Playwright Chromium: `new ArrayBuffer(1536MB)` → ok, `new ArrayBuffer(2048MB)` → FAIL, but 16×256 MB buffers held simultaneously → 4096 MB ok. Same probe under Node 25: 1024/2048/4096 MB all ok. File sizes on disk: ernie.msh 184,207,351 B; Thalamus_TI.msh 255,005,467 B; ernie_seeg.msh 492,090,201 B.
findings.fix: Replace the §5 IPC arrow. Preferred: pair the `app://` scheme from the file:// finding with `protocol.handle` returning a streaming `Response`, and have the **worker** do `fetch('app://file/<encoded path>')` directly — bytes never touch the UI thread, streaming avoids one full copy, and the same code path works in a browser. Alternative: `nodeIntegrationInWorker: true` and let the worker `require('fs')` + `zlib` itself. Either way state explicitly in §5 that (i) the UI thread never holds the raw file bytes, (ii) the renderer must never allocate a single buffer > 1 GB — chunk uploads of large volumes into the 3D texture with `texSubImage3D` slabs, and (iii) `openFile` returns a path + size, not bytes. Add a §9 row: "open `ernie_seeg.msh` (492 MB)" so the largest local file is actually exercised.

findings.title: Phase 0's gate does not produce the interface stubs Phase 1's four parallel agents need, so three of them start blocked
findings.claim: Phase 1 runs four agents in parallel (crates, wasm+worker glue, engine, app). As written, the app agent has nothing to code against — §8 says "Everything the UI can do must be reachable from `engine` API alone" but no engine API is specified anywhere in the contract. The engine agent cannot typecheck against `@tetravox/wasm` because `packages/wasm/pkg` is generated and git-ignored and is being written concurrently. The wasm agent cannot compile `tvx-wasm` until `tvx-nifti`/`tvx-mesh-io`/`tvx-geom` expose their types. Phase 0's gate ("a triangle whose colour came from a WASM call") does not force any of these to exist.
findings.evidence: ROADMAP Phase 0 bullet list contains no interface deliverable. §2 marks `packages/wasm/pkg` as "(generated, git-ignored)". ARCHITECTURE has no `Engine` interface. Confirmed the repo currently contains only `AGENTS.md` and `docs/` — nothing is scaffolded yet, so all of this is still cheap to add.
findings.fix: Add to the Phase-0 gate: "the following files exist, compile, and are frozen — changing them requires an ARCHITECTURE.md edit in the same commit": (1) `packages/protocol/src/index.ts` — the worker envelope (see the protocol finding); (2) `packages/engine/src/scene/types.ts` — §4's Dataset/Layer/Scene types, zero imports; (3) `packages/engine/src/api.ts` — the `Engine` facade (`create(canvas)`, `addDataset`, `removeDataset`, `addLayer`, `updateLayer(id, patch)`, `reorderLayers`, `setCursor`, `setLayout`, `setView(viewId, camera)`, `pick(viewId,x,y)`, `probe(world)`, `readPixel(viewId,x,y)`, `screenshot(opts)`, `toViewSpec()`, `loadViewSpec()`, `on(event, cb)`) plus the event-name union (`'cursor'|'pick'|'layers'|'datasets'|'progress'|'frame'|'error'`) and a `MockEngine` that satisfies it with no GL, so the app agent builds and tests the entire UI in Phase 1 without the engine; (4) every Rust signature from §6.1–§6.3 present as `todo!()` stubs so `cargo check --workspace` is green on day 1 of Phase 1; (5) `packages/wasm/src/index.ts` re-exporting the client interface, with `pkg` behind a build script so the engine agent never imports generated code directly.

findings.title: Golden screenshots will not be portable between the CI renderer and any developer machine, and the contract does not say which one is authoritative
findings.claim: §1 mandates "Playwright (Chromium headless **and** Electron) with pixel assertions" and §10 requires a golden PNG per rendering feature, but nothing pins the renderer. Headless Chromium renders through SwiftShader; a developer running headed on macOS renders through ANGLE/Metal. These are not merely different in anti-aliasing — they expose different capability sets, so shaders can legitimately take different paths. Goldens captured on one will never match the other, and Playwright's default snapshot naming appends a platform suffix, so an agent that regenerates a golden on macOS silently creates a second file instead of fixing the failing one. Without a rule, agents will regenerate goldens to make red turn green, which destroys the only rendering verification the project has.
findings.evidence: Measured the same page under Playwright 1.62.1 Chromium three ways. headless (default): UNMASKED_RENDERER `ANGLE (Google, Vulkan 1.3.0 (SwiftShader Device …), SwiftShader driver)`, MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE 8192, MAX_DRAW_BUFFERS 6, 29 extensions, `EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2` **absent**. headed on M2 Max: `ANGLE (Apple, ANGLE Metal Renderer: Apple M2 Max)`, MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE 16384, MAX_DRAW_BUFFERS 8, 36 extensions, timer query **present**. Adding `--use-gl=angle --use-angle=swiftshader-webgl --enable-unsafe-swiftshader` changed nothing in headless — Playwright's headless Chromium already resolves to SwiftShader with no flags on this Playwright version.
findings.fix: Write a §11 "Rendering verification" section. (a) Goldens are captured **only** under headless Chromium/SwiftShader at a fixed canvas size and `deviceScaleFactor: 1`, with the Playwright version pinned exactly (it pins the SwiftShader build); regenerating a golden requires a commit message body stating what changed visually. (b) Compare with `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.002` and `threshold: 0.15`, not byte equality — SwiftShader's LLVM JIT is not bit-identical across arm64 macOS and x86_64 Linux, so pick **one** CI job (ubuntu-24.04) as the golden authority and have the macOS job run the same tests with a looser ratio. (c) Add `--force-device-scale-factor=1 --disable-lcd-text --font-render-hinting=none --hide-scrollbars` to the launch args. (d) Make the engine expose a `deterministic` mode that disables the timer query, fixes the frame clock, and renders synchronously so `requestRender()` completes before the screenshot. (e) Because SwiftShader lacks the timer query, §7.1's `Timer` must be optional and the status bar must degrade, not crash.

findings.title: Most rendering correctness can be proven analytically rather than by golden images — the contract should say so, or agents will over-rely on PNGs they cannot judge
findings.claim: AGENTS.md rule 1 says "Look at the PNG", which an agent cannot meaningfully do. A golden PNG proves only "same as last time"; it never proves "correct", so the first golden an agent commits enshrines whatever it built, including a wrong colormap, a flipped axis, or a radiological/neurological mix-up — precisely the class of bug that matters here and that §3 spends a paragraph on. The contract has no mechanism that would catch left/right being mirrored.
findings.evidence: §9 promises "Rendering has Playwright screenshot tests with pixel assertions at known positions" but defines neither the helper nor what the expected values are derived from. §3 defines neurological vs radiological display but no test is specified that would distinguish them.
findings.fix: Add to §11: every rendering feature ships **two** tests. (1) An *analytic* pixel assertion whose expected RGBA is computed from first principles, not from a previous run — e.g. a synthetic 4×4×4 volume with value `v = i` under colormap `gray`, window `[0,3]`, so the pixel at the cursor must be exactly `rgb(85,85,85)` ±1; a 4-tet mesh with tag colours from a fixture LUT so the cap pixel is exactly the tag colour. Provide `expectPixel(view, x, y, [r,g,b,a], tol)` backed by an engine `readPixel` call (no PNG round-trip). (2) A golden PNG for regression only. Add three mandatory orientation tests using an **asymmetric** synthetic volume (a bright cube in the left-anterior-superior octant only): assert the bright pixel is on the screen-left in neurological mode and screen-right after the radiological toggle, in each of the three 2D views. Also add a fixture-expectations JSON: `scripts/gen-fixtures.py` writes `testdata/expected.json` (node counts, per-tag element counts, field min/mean/max, voxel values at listed indices) computed with nibabel, committed, so the Rust real-data tests assert numbers without needing Python at test time.

findings.title: Gmsh v2 binary parsing details that decide the reader's structure are absent, and one stated rule is wrong for cropped meshes
findings.claim: §6.2 gives a one-line signature and a rule ("`$ElementData` is given in file element order … → split into per-kind vectors") that hides the parts that actually take the time and that will differ between the reader an agent writes and the data on disk. Not stated: v2 binary `$Elements` is a sequence of blocks each headed by `(elm_type, numElems, numTags)` as three int32 with a per-block record stride of `1 + numTags + nodesPerElem` — a reader that assumes 2 tags will desynchronise on any file that uses a different count. Not stated: `$NodeData`/`$ElementData` records are `(int32 id, float64 × ncomp)` — **id-keyed and float64**, so "file element order" is an assumption that holds for the whole-head files but is not something the format guarantees, and the `Field { data: Vec<f32> }` downcast from f64 is an undocumented decision. Not stated: node coordinates are float64 in the file. Also, `$PhysicalNames` is listed as a source of tag names, but the actual SimNIBS meshes do not contain that section at all.
findings.evidence: Parsed `m2m_ernie/ernie.msh` directly: `$MeshFormat` = `2.2 1 8`; two element blocks, `type=2 n=1177213 ntags=2` then `type=4 n=4722625 ntags=2`; 847,165 nodes with contiguous ids. `grep -c PhysicalNames ernie.msh` → 0 (no `$PhysicalNames` section). SimNIBS's own reader (`mesh_io.py` `_read_msh_2`) reads `elm_type, nr, _ = np.fromfile(f,'int32',3)` — it discards `numTags` and hardcodes 2 — and its data readers use `dt = np.dtype([('id', np.int32), ('values', np.float64, nr_comp)])`, i.e. id-keyed f64. Same reader raises `IOError` for version 4, so SimNIBS cannot be used to cross-check a v4.1 reader at all.
findings.fix: Expand §6.2 with the block layout and the record layouts above; state that the reader honours `numTags` and builds an `elmNumber → index` map (fast-path when ids are 1..N contiguous, which is the SimNIBS case) rather than assuming positional order; state that field values are read as f64 and stored as f32, and node coords likewise. Replace "`$PhysicalNames`" with: names and colours come from `$PhysicalNames` when present, else from a sibling `<mesh>_LUT.txt` (SimNIBS `#No. Label Name: R G B A`), else from the sibling `<mesh>.msh.opt` (`Physical Volume(" GM",2)` + `Mesh.Color.<Ordinal>`), else a deterministic palette — and add the rule `surfaceTag 1xxx inherits the colour of volumeTag (1xxx − 1000)`, which is exactly what SimNIBS's LUT and .opt encode. Also flag in DECISIONS.md that Gmsh 4.1 support has no reference implementation locally (SimNIBS refuses v4) and no sample file, so it must be generated with the bundled `gmsh` CLI at `~/Applications/SimNIBS-4.6/bin/gmsh` or dropped from v1.

findings.title: GIfTI's "GZipBase64Binary" is zlib, not gzip — and the XML dependency is undeclared
findings.claim: `read_gifti` is one line in the contract. The test-data GIfTI files store their arrays as `Encoding="GZipBase64Binary"`, and despite the name the payload after base64-decoding is a raw **zlib** stream (`78 9c`), not a gzip stream (`1f 8b`). A Rust reader that reaches for `flate2::read::GzDecoder` — the natural choice given §5 already talks about sniffing the `1f 8b` magic for `.nii.gz` — fails on every surface file in the dataset. §6.2 also does not mention that GIfTI is XML, which means an XML parser (`quick-xml` or similar) is a new dependency requiring a DECISIONS.md line per AGENTS.md rule 5, nor that `ExternalFileBinary` and plain `Base64Binary` encodings exist.
findings.evidence: `m2m_ernie/surfaces/lh.central.gii`: `Encoding="GZipBase64Binary" Endian="LittleEndian"`. Python `gzip.decompress(base64.b64decode(data))` → `BadGzipFile: Not a gzipped file (b'x\x9c')`; `zlib.decompress(...)` succeeds, yielding 737,286 float32 (245,762 × 3) and 1,474,560 int32 triangle indices. `CoordinateSystemTransformMatrix` is present in the file.
findings.fix: In §6.2, spell out: GIfTI is XML; supported encodings are `ASCII`, `Base64Binary`, `GZipBase64Binary` (**zlib stream, use `ZlibDecoder`, not `GzDecoder`**) and `ExternalFileBinary` (reject with `Unsupported` in v1); honour `Endian`; apply `CoordinateSystemTransformMatrix` when present. Add `quick-xml` (and `base64`) to §2's dependency list and DECISIONS.md now, so no Phase-1 agent has to make that call alone.

findings.title: AGENTS.md misstates the test data, so real-data tests written against it will fail on facts
findings.claim: Three claims in the test-data section are wrong or incomplete, and an agent writing the mandatory real-data tests (AGENTS.md rule 2) will encode them as assertions. (1) `Thalamus_TI.msh` is described as having "element fields incl. `TI_max`, vector `E`" — it contains exactly one `$ElementData` field, `TI_max`, scalar, and no vector field. (2) tags are described as "1–10 / 1001–1010" — tag 4 does not exist in the mesh, and tag **1099** (Internal_air_surface, 51,582 triangles) does exist. (3) `grey_Thalamus_TI.msh` is described as "GM tets only" without noting the consequence: it has **no triangles at all**, so any code path that assumes a mesh has a renderable surface without running boundary extraction produces an empty 3D view for it.
findings.fix: Correct the AGENTS.md bullets with these exact numbers and add them as the reference values for the real-data tests: `ernie.msh` → 847165 nodes, 1177213 tris, 4722625 tets, the per-tag counts above, bbox as above; `Thalamus_TI.msh` → one scalar field `TI_max`, min 1.086e-12, max 10.29; `grey_Thalamus_TI.msh` → 368762 nodes, 1340029 tets, 0 tris, `TI_max` 0.01027…0.5451; `lh.central.gii` → 245762 vertices, 491520 triangles, already in subject world mm. Add the note that `grey_*.msh` is a tets-only mesh and is the canonical test for the boundary-extraction path.

findings.title: The Phase-1 gate can be met without building tet topology at all — say so, or the critical path is 3× longer than it needs to be
findings.claim: The Phase-1 gate is "tissue surfaces of ernie.msh orbiting", and §6.3 routes that through `build_topology` (unique-face extraction over 4.7 M tets) then `tag_surfaces(mesh, topo)`. But SimNIBS meshes already *contain* the tissue surfaces as triangle elements with tags 1001–1010 — 1.18 M triangles, ready to draw with zero geometry work. Deriving the same surfaces from the tets is slower, produces a different (and duplicated) surface, and puts the single largest and riskiest piece of `tvx-geom` on the critical path for first pixels. Meanwhile the case that genuinely needs boundary extraction (`grey_*.msh`, tets only) is not in the gate at all.
findings.evidence: Element census above: `ernie.msh` carries 1,177,213 triangles in tags 1001–1010 plus 1099, one per tissue interface, alongside the 4.7 M tets. `grey_Thalamus_TI.msh` carries 1,340,029 tets and zero triangles. Parsing the full 176 MB `ernie.msh` element+node structure with numpy took 0.31 s wall on this machine, so the §6.2 targets (<1.5 s native / <3 s WASM) are comfortable — the topology build is the part at risk, not the parse.
findings.fix: State in §7.4 and §6.3 that the **default 3D representation of a mesh that has surface elements is its own tagged triangles**; `build_topology` + `boundary_faces` is required only (a) for meshes with no triangles, and (b) after isolation or clipping changes which tets are visible. Split the Phase-1 gate accordingly: "ernie.msh tag-surfaces orbiting" (no topology needed) as the Phase-1 gate, and move "grey_Thalamus_TI.msh boundary extracted from tets in < 1.5 s" into Phase 2 alongside isolation, where it belongs. This takes `build_topology` off the path to first pixels for three other agents.

findings.title: pnpm 10 skips dependency build scripts by default and Electron fetches its binary lazily — a fresh clone and an offline CI both break in confusing ways
findings.claim: AGENTS.md's first command is `pnpm install`, and Phase 0 sets up electron-vite + Playwright. On pnpm 10 (the installed version), lifecycle scripts of dependencies are **not** run unless allowlisted, so esbuild — which electron-vite and Vite both depend on — is installed without its platform binary and Vite fails at first use with an error that does not mention pnpm. Separately, `electron@44` has no postinstall at all; it downloads its ~100 MB binary on **first launch**, which means a CI job that installs with a warm cache and then runs `pnpm e2e` needs outbound network at test time, and a sandboxed agent environment will see the launch simply fail.
findings.evidence: Reproduced locally with pnpm 10.30.3: `pnpm install` of `esbuild@0.25.0` prints `Warning ─ Ignored build scripts: esbuild@0.25.0. Run "pnpm approve-builds"…`. For electron: `node -e "require('electron/package.json').scripts"` → `undefined`; after `npm i -D electron@44`, `node_modules/electron/dist` does not exist until the first `npx electron`, which prints `Downloading Electron binary...`.
findings.fix: Make the root `package.json` scaffold in Phase 0 include `"pnpm": { "onlyBuiltDependencies": ["esbuild", "electron", "electron-winstaller"] }` (extend as native deps are added) and add a Phase-0 gate item: "a clean clone with an empty pnpm store reaches `pnpm e2e` green". In CI, cache `~/.cache/electron` and `~/.cache/ms-playwright` and add an explicit `pnpm exec electron --version` warm-up step before the e2e job so a download failure surfaces as its own red step. Add this to AGENTS.md §Commands so agents do not each rediscover it.

findings.title: Parallel worktrees will collide on the two generated lockfiles, which AGENTS.md's "only append" rule does not cover
findings.claim: Rule 3 says shared files are "pre-populated by the scaffold; only append", naming the workspace `Cargo.toml` and root `package.json`. It does not name `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `Cargo.lock`, which are machine-generated, not append-structured, and will be touched by every one of the four Phase-1 agents the moment any of them adds a dependency (and §6.2/§6.3 imply several: an XML parser, a base64 decoder, miniz_oxide, thiserror, criterion, wasm-bindgen). Every merge to main will conflict in both files, and the naive resolution (accept one side) silently drops the other agent's dependency, producing a failure at build time on main rather than in the PR.
findings.evidence: AGENTS.md rule 3 text; §2's crate list requires per-crate dependencies; §5 names `miniz_oxide`; §6 names `thiserror`; §1 names `gl-matrix`; §6.2 implicitly needs an XML parser and base64.
findings.fix: Two changes. (1) Declare a **dependency freeze at the end of Phase 0**: the scaffold commits every crate and package dependency Phase 1 will need — `thiserror`, `miniz_oxide`/`flate2`, `quick-xml`, `base64`, `byteorder`, `wasm-bindgen`, `js-sys`, `criterion`, `gl-matrix`, `zustand`, `react`, `vitest`, `@playwright/test`, `electron`, `electron-vite`, `electron-builder` — with both lockfiles committed and green. Adding one after that is a coordinated change, not an incidental one. (2) Add to rule 3: "`pnpm-lock.yaml` and `Cargo.lock` are never merged; on conflict, take main's version and re-run `pnpm install` / `cargo check --workspace` to regenerate."

findings.title: CI is specified as "macOS + Ubuntu" but the artefacts the project promises cannot all be produced from those two jobs
findings.claim: Phase 3's gate is "`.dmg` + `.AppImage` + `.deb` open ernie", and §2 describes a single macOS + Ubuntu workflow. Two problems. (a) AppImage and .deb cannot be produced from macOS — they must be built on Linux or in the electron-builder Docker image — so a maintainer running `pnpm package` on the dev machine gets only the .dmg, and the roadmap does not say the Linux artefacts are CI-only. (b) `macos-latest` is now macOS 26 **arm64**; an Intel .dmg needs a separate `macos-26-intel` job. The matrix also silently decides which architecture the golden screenshots come from, which the verification finding depends on.
findings.evidence: electron-builder documentation: "Don't expect that you can build an app for all platforms on one platform"; AppImages must be built on Linux or via the electronuserland/builder Docker image. GitHub runner-images README: `macos-latest` = macOS 26 Arm64; Intel is `macos-26-intel`/`macos-26-large`; `ubuntu-latest` = Ubuntu 24.04 x64, with `ubuntu-24.04-arm` available separately. Docker is available on this machine (server 29.1.3, linux/aarch64), so the Docker route is viable locally but produces arm64 Linux artefacts, not x64.
findings.fix: Replace §2's one-line CI note with an explicit matrix and write it into the Phase-3 gate: `test` job on `ubuntu-24.04` (cargo test, wasm build, vitest, Playwright — **golden authority**) and on `macos-latest` (same, loose pixel tolerance); `package` jobs on `macos-latest` → arm64 .dmg, `macos-26-intel` → x64 .dmg, `ubuntu-24.04` → x64 .AppImage + .deb, optionally `ubuntu-24.04-arm` → arm64 Linux. State that `pnpm package` on macOS produces macOS artefacts only and that Linux artefacts come from CI (or `docker run electronuserland/builder`). Add an artefact smoke test — launch the packaged binary with a CLI arg pointing at a fixture and assert it exits 0 after rendering one frame — since "opens ernie" is otherwise unverifiable by an agent.

findings.title: Unsigned macOS builds are effectively undistributable on current macOS, and no signing decision is recorded
findings.claim: The roadmap ships a `.dmg` with no mention of signing or notarisation. On macOS Sequoia and later, Apple removed the Control-click-to-open Gatekeeper bypass, so a user who downloads an unsigned .dmg gets a hard "cannot be opened" dialog and must know to go to System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway. electron-builder's two non-Developer-ID options are both traps: `mac.sign.identity: "-"` (ad-hoc) produces a bundle that only runs on the machine that built it and has known regressions in current electron-builder around entitlements, while `identity: null` produces a fully unsigned bundle that arm64 macOS treats as broken. This is a distribution decision, not an implementation detail, and it changes what Phase 3 has to build (auto-update, for instance, is impossible unsigned).
findings.evidence: Apple removed the Control-click Gatekeeper override in macOS Sequoia; users must now dismiss the dialog and use System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway. electron-builder docs: `mac.sign.identity: "-"` = ad-hoc, "the app will only run on the machine that built it"; `identity: null` skips signing. electron-builder issue #9529 documents an ad-hoc-signing regression between 26.0.12 and 26.0.13 (current published version is 26.15.3). Installed Electron latest is 44.0.0.
findings.fix: Add a DECISIONS.md line now with one of: (a) Developer ID + notarisation (needs a $99/yr account, `APPLE_ID`/`APPLE_APP_SPECIFIC_PASSWORD`/`APPLE_TEAM_ID` secrets, and `notarize: true` in electron-builder) — the only option that gives a clean double-click install and enables auto-update; or (b) explicitly unsigned, in which case USER_GUIDE.md must carry the System Settings walkthrough and a `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Tetravox.app` one-liner, and Phase 3 must drop auto-update from scope. Also pin `electron-builder` to a specific patch version in the scaffold rather than a caret range, given the ad-hoc-signing regressions. On Linux, add a matching note that the AppImage needs `--no-sandbox` or a correctly-owned `chrome-sandbox`, and that Electron will fall back to software rendering on machines without a usable GL driver — the app should detect `UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL` containing "SwiftShader" at startup and warn, rather than silently running at 2 fps.

findings.title: §4's Scene is claimed to be JSON-serialisable but holds TypedArrays and a WebGLTexture
findings.claim: §4 ends with "`Scene` = `{ datasets, layers, … }` and is JSON-serialisable (`ViewSpec`) so a scene can be saved, reloaded, and rendered headlessly." But `datasets` per the same section contain `data: TypedArray`, `nodes: Float32Array`, `gpu: { texture: WebGLTexture }` and an opaque worker `handle`. None of that survives `JSON.stringify`, and a `WebGLTexture` also ties the dataset type to one GL context, which conflicts with §7.5's per-view cameras and any future second context. Two agents will disagree about whether `toViewSpec()` walks the live Scene or a parallel structure.
findings.evidence: §4 type definitions versus the serialisability claim in the same section; §8 specifies `*.tetravox.json` (ViewSpec) as a user-facing save format.
findings.fix: Separate the two types explicitly in §4: `Scene` is the runtime graph (holds arrays, GPU handles, worker handles); `ViewSpec` is the persisted form and references datasets **by path + a content hash**, never by data, plus all layer display parameters, camera state, cursor, layout and the radiological flag. Give the exact `ViewSpec` JSON shape and a `version: 1` field in §4, since it is a user-facing file format and a headless-render input. Move `gpu` out of `VolumeDataset` into an engine-private `GpuResources` map keyed by `DatasetId`, so the dataset type stays plain data and remains transferable between worker and UI.

findings.title: wasm-pack's output cannot be a pnpm workspace package as drawn, and its build pulls two binaries from the network
findings.claim: §2 describes `packages/wasm` as "@tetravox/wasm — build output of tvx-wasm (generated, git-ignored) + TS worker glue". Two mechanical problems. (a) wasm-pack writes its own `pkg/package.json` with `"name"` taken from the **crate** name and drops a `.gitignore` containing `*` into `pkg/`, so `pkg` cannot itself be the `@tetravox/wasm` workspace package and cannot be resolved by pnpm on a clone where it does not yet exist — the hand-written package must wrap it. (b) wasm-pack downloads the `wasm-bindgen` CLI and `wasm-opt` at build time; if the downloaded CLI version drifts from the `wasm-bindgen` crate version in `Cargo.lock`, the build fails with a version-mismatch error that reads like a code bug.
findings.evidence: Built a probe crate with the installed wasm-pack 0.15.0: output is `pkg/{package.json, tvxprobe.js, tvxprobe.d.ts, tvxprobe_bg.wasm, tvxprobe_bg.wasm.d.ts, .gitignore}`; `pkg/package.json` → `"name": "tvxprobe"`; `pkg/.gitignore` is 1 byte (`*`). Build log: `[INFO]: ⬇️  Installing wasm-bindgen...` then `[INFO]: Optimizing wasm binaries with wasm-opt...`. Compiled `wasm-bindgen v0.2.127`; local toolchain is cargo 1.93.0 with `wasm32-unknown-unknown` installed.
findings.fix: In §2, state that `packages/wasm` is a hand-written package with its own committed `package.json` (`"name": "@tetravox/wasm"`) whose `src/` imports from `./pkg/tvx_wasm.js` — a git-ignored build output, never a workspace member. Add a `postinstall`-free `pnpm wasm` prerequisite to `pnpm build`/`pnpm test`/`pnpm typecheck` so no agent ever typechecks against a missing `pkg`, and check in a generated `pkg/tvx_wasm.d.ts` **stub** at Phase 0 so `tsc` works before the first wasm build. Pin `wasm-bindgen` exactly in `Cargo.toml` (`=0.2.127`) and pin wasm-pack's version in `scripts/build-wasm.sh`; cache `~/.cache/.wasm-pack` in CI.

findings.title: wasm32's 4 GiB ceiling and the topology working set deserve an explicit memory budget in §9
findings.claim: §9 targets "memory < 1.5 GB" for ernie without saying which memory. The WASM linear memory is hard-capped at 4 GiB and never shrinks once grown, Rust on wasm32 caps a single allocation at `isize::MAX` (2 GiB), and the sort-based unique-face extraction in §6.3 has a working set that is not obviously under the bar: 4,722,625 tets × 4 faces = 18.89 M face records, each needing a ~12-byte canonical key plus a 4-byte payload, plus scratch for a non-in-place radix sort — roughly 600 MB peak — on top of the mesh arrays and, if the file bytes are still held, another 176 MB. Two agents making independent choices (hold the file bytes vs stream; radix vs in-place sort) can land either side of the limit, and the failure mode is an unrecoverable `RuntimeError: Out of memory` that poisons the module.
findings.evidence: Measured in Chromium: `new WebAssembly.Memory({initial:1, maximum:65537})` → `value 65537 is above the upper bound 65536` (i.e. 4 GiB hard cap); memory64 unsupported (`new WebAssembly.Memory({initial:1, address:'i64'})` → `Cannot convert 1 to a BigInt`). Renderer-side single ArrayBuffer > ~1.5 GB fails to allocate. `ernie.msh` census: 847,165 nodes, 4,722,625 tets, 1,177,213 tris.
findings.fix: Add a memory-budget row to §9 broken out by arena — "WASM linear memory ≤ 1.2 GB, renderer JS heap ≤ 400 MB, GPU ≤ 500 MB for the ernie scene" — and instrument it: expose `performance.memory`-independent numbers via `wasm.memory.buffer.byteLength` and a `gl.getExtension('WEBGL_debug_shaders')`-free GPU estimate, reported in the status bar (§8 already promises a GPU memory estimate). Add two rules to §6.3: the file bytes are dropped before topology is built, and unique-face extraction must be a radix sort over a packed `u64` key (the three sorted vertex indices fit in 3×21 bits for meshes under 2 M nodes; fall back to a 96-bit key with an explicit second pass above that) so the scratch buffer is 8 bytes/face, not 16. Add an explicit `Error::OutOfMemory` and a client rule that an OOM tears down and recreates the worker rather than leaving a poisoned module.

reviews.verdict: The contract is unusually strong on domain substance — the coordinate rules, the layer model and the perf bars are the right ones, and the real data confirms the parsing and performance targets are achievable. It is weak exactly where an agent-built project fails: the seams between agents. Three things will stop the product as written — a packaged Electron app cannot start the compute worker or load the wasm at all over `file://` (verified experimentally), the label-LUT design cannot represent FreeSurfer or `.annot` ids so the atlas requirement fails, and the cap API takes one plane while the layer model promises six. Beyond those, the worker protocol, the engine facade and the golden-screenshot policy are entirely unspecified, which means Phase 1's four parallel agents have nothing to build against and no way to prove rendering is right; Phase 0's gate should be extended to freeze those interfaces before any of them start.

     up: vec3;       // unit, in-plane, screen up. Re-orthogonalise on load: up ← normalize(up − (up·n)n); reject if |up×n| < 1e-4

4. **A concrete numeric collision the finding didn't spot, which makes the fix mandatory rather than nice-to-have.** The stated dev machine is a MacBook Pro Liquid Retina XDR (ProMotion, up to 120 Hz; confirmed via `system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType`), and Chrome drives rAF at display rate. The frame budget on the machine §7.2 names is therefore **8.3 ms**, and §7.2 spends **8 ms of it on the render alone** — zero headroom for the upload, the worker-result copy, the React re-render, or the probe. §7.2's own target is self-defeating unless the refresh rate it is stated against is pinned.

5. **The reviewer overstates §9 slightly** (worth correcting, not fatal): §9 *does* have two interaction-phase rows ("Cut-plane drag (cap recompute + upload) ≥ 30 fps end-to-end", "Slice scrub … 60 fps"). But neither says at what quality level, so once any adaptive fallback exists both rows become unbenchmarkable, and neither measures latency.

6. **The under-appreciated consequence: it breaks the test strategy.** AGENTS.md rule 1 and §10 make Playwright pixel screenshots the sole verification for all rendering work, and ROADMAP gates Phases 1-3 on them. A time-based `interacting`/settle state with adaptive quality makes every golden screenshot racy unless the engine exposes an explicit "settled and fully rendered" promise for tests to await. Any fix that adds adaptive quality without that hook will produce a flaky suite across all three phases.

I did check one plausible refutation angle and it failed: I suspected §7.1's `Timer (EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2 when available)` was dead on macOS (Apple GL exposes no timestamp queries), which would have made the status-bar "frame ms" sub-claim much sharper. It is in fact exposed on ANGLE-Metal here (`getSupportedExtensions()` includes `EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2`; also `MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE` 2048, `MAX_SAMPLES` 4). So the GPU-timer angle should not be used as support; the status-bar sub-claim reduces to the (still true, still cheap) point that fps is undefined when nothing renders.

Net: the finding is material — it changes what gets built (a pump module, an interaction state in the engine API, a settle hook the whole Playwright suite depends on, and two rewritten §9 rows) — and it is cheapest to fix now, before Phase 1 writes `render-on-demand` into `packages/engine`.

The finding's core survives (the §1 parity claim is unverified and §9/Phase-0 are unfalsifiable as written), but three of its sub-claims are factually wrong and the most important one is wrong in a way that makes the problem WORSE, not milder. Verified with documentation lookups plus two live Chromium experiments.

REFUTED — sub-claim "falls back to SwiftShader silently": that behaviour was removed. Chromium deprecated automatic SwiftShader WebGL fallback in M130 (console warning) and REMOVED it on desktop in M137 (chromestatus 5166674414927872 / blink-dev "Intent to Remove: SwiftShader Fallback"; https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/gpu/swiftshader.md). Today `canvas.getContext('webgl2')` returns **null** on a blocklisted/GPU-less machine unless the process is launched with `--enable-unsafe-swiftshader`. So the Linux risk is not "quietly 5 fps", it is "Tetravox opens a blank window and every view is dead". The reviewer's proposed fix (a "reduced-quality profile" when the renderer is SwiftShader) is unreachable in a default Electron build — there is nothing to detect, because there is no context.

REFUTED — sub-claim "Wayland needs explicit ozone flags": stale. Electron 38.2+ is Wayland-native out of the box; `ELECTRON_OZONE_PLATFORM_HINT` was *removed* in Electron 38 (electronjs.org/blog/tech-talk-wayland). This reduces to a version floor, not a design change.

REFUTED — sub-claim "the design now depends on three extensions": ARCHITECTURE.md mentions none of them. I grepped: no `clip_cull`, no `norm16`, no `float_linear`, no `getSupportedExtensions` anywhere in docs/. §7.4 explicitly specifies `discard`-based clipping ("up to 6 planes as vec4 uniforms; discard on the clipped side"), i.e. the contract deliberately does NOT use WEBGL_clip_cull_distance — the reviewer measured their own spike, not the contract. Of the three, only OES_texture_float_linear is *implied*, by §7.3's "sampler3D (trilinear) for scalars" over the §4 `R32F` format; that one is a genuine (if near-universal) unstated requirement, since float filtering is an extension in WebGL2 core (MDN OES_texture_float_linear).

SURVIVES — §9 has no reference machine. Independently confirmed the reviewer's numbers came from the top of the range: my probe returns `ANGLE (Apple, ANGLE Metal Renderer: Apple M2 Max)`. "60 fps on Apple M-series" spans ~4× GPU throughput, so §9's own promise ("measured, not asserted") is not testable.

SURVIVES, restated — Phase 0's "(headless, swiftshader ok)" is wrong in both directions, and I measured it. Launching Playwright's bundled Chromium 151 headless on macOS with default args, with `--enable-unsafe-swiftshader`, and with `--use-angle=metal` all produced the **same** renderer: ANGLE Metal on the real GPU (36 extensions, `OES_texture_float_linear`/`EXT_texture_norm16`/`WEBGL_clip_cull_distance`/`EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2` all present). So (a) the macOS CI leg never uses SwiftShader and will bake hardware-Metal goldens, and (b) the Ubuntu leg on a GPU-less GitHub runner will, post-M137, get a null WebGL2 context and fail on `gl === null` before any pixel comparison happens. Phase 0's gate as written cannot go green on Ubuntu.

TWO ADDITIONAL DEFECTS the finding gestures at but misses, both confirmed by experiment and both silent-failure classes:
1. §4 declares `gpu.format: 'R8'|'R16UI'|'R32F'|'RGBA8'` while §7.3/§4 offer per-layer `interpolation:'linear'|'nearest'`. Integer formats are not texture-filterable in GLES3. I bound an R16UI 3D texture with LINEAR min/mag: `usampler3D` sampled **0 with GL error 0** (incomplete texture → silent black), and `sampler3D` on the same texture gave **INVALID_OPERATION (1282)** with the draw dropped. The primary test volume `m2m_ernie/T1.nii.gz` is int16, so the very first real dataset hits this. Without EXT_texture_norm16 (`R16`, filterable, 2 B/voxel) the only filterable path is R32F at 2× VRAM — which is exactly the extension the reviewer wrongly claimed was already a dependency.
2. No texture-size limit anywhere in the contract. MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE is 2048 on this M2 Max/ANGLE; the GLES3/WebGL2 guaranteed minimum is 256. §4's "one 3D texture per volume" has no query, no downsample, no bricking path, so a 512³+ CT or a large atlas fails with no defined behaviour.

I tried to refute this and could not — the core defect is real and I measured it. But three of the finding's supporting claims are factually wrong, and the proposed fix is wrong in shape, so the fix needs replacing rather than adopting.

WHAT SURVIVES (measured on /Users/idohaber/datasets/000/derivatives/SimNIBS/sub-ernie/m2m_ernie/ernie.msh, parsed directly from $Elements)

1. Depth complexity. I cast 400 random rays per surface and counted triangle crossings:
   - tag 1002 (GM): median 4 (axial) / 6 (sagittal), p90 8-10, max 18; 79-86% of rays cross more than twice.
   - tag 1001 (WM): median 6-8, p90 10-12, max 18; 85-91% >2.
   - tag 1005 (scalp): median 2, p90 2, max 5-6; only 3-9% >2.
   §7.2's "back-to-front per object" is a no-op for a single translucent GM shell, so ~80% of pixels blend in submission order. Confirmed.

2. A second defect the finding did not name, and it is worse. "Back-to-front per object" is not merely insufficient for non-convex objects — it is *ill-defined* for concentric ones. Area-weighted centroids: WM-GM 4.3 mm apart, GM-CSF 11.2 mm, while their radial extents overlap by ~90 mm and their depth ranges interpenetrate by ±100 mm at a ~400 mm camera distance. No per-object key (centroid or bbox) can order nested shells. This is the iconic head render (scalp+skull+GM all translucent) and the contract has no answer for it.

3. Caps. §7.2 puts cut caps in the opaque pass unconditionally, while §7.4 says caps are "drawn with the same material" and §4 has `capColorMode:'inherit'`. Direct contradiction when the owning layer has opacity<1. Confirmed.

WHAT IS WRONG IN THE FINDING

4. The tissue labels are swapped. Triangle counts are exact, the mapping is not. By extent, area and enclosed volume: 1001 = WM (249,245 tris, 2201 cm², encloses 603 cm³), 1002 = GM (335,930 tris, 1947 cm², 1309 cm³), 1005 = scalp (77,032 tris, largest extent 167.8x228.6x228.8, encloses 4841 cm³), 1007 = compact bone, 1008 = spongy bone. So the gyrified cortical surface is 335,930 triangles, not 77,032 — 4.4x the finding's number, which matters for any per-triangle-sort option.

5. "cullFace(FRONT) then cullFace(BACK) ... is exactly correct for a closed manifold" is FALSE. Exactness needs <=2 crossings per ray, i.e. convexity, not closedness. At GM median 4-6 and max 18, two-pass fixes only the outermost back/front pair and leaves the rest interleaved arbitrarily inside each phase.

6. The headline scenario is the least broken case, not the most. For "translucent skin over a field-coloured cortex": the scalp is effectively convex (median 2 crossings, 91-97% of rays <=2), and with the cortex opaque, the opaque pass writes depth so the scalp's own back faces are depth-rejected almost everywhere — leaving one blended fragment, which the contract as written already gets right. The genuinely broken case is a *translucent gyrified surface* (GM/WM at opacity<1 to see a deep target or an E-field hotspot), which the finding treats as secondary.

7. A blocker the finding's fix would trip over. Both `backfaceCull` and any front/back split assume outward winding, and ernie's file triangles are not uniformly wound. Origin-independent signed volumes (recomputed about three origins, signs stable): 1001 -603, 1002 -1309, 1003 -1495, 1099 -75 cm^3 (inward) vs 1005 +4841, 1007 +2333, 1008 +112, 1009 +66, 1006 +19 cm^3 (outward). Magnitudes match plausible anatomy, so these are genuinely near-closed shells with a definite global orientation that differs by tag. None is watertight: 974-2920 non-manifold/boundary edges each. §6.3's `boundary_faces` is specified "outward-oriented" so ernie's *default* path (surfaces rebuilt from tets) is safe, but `read_msh` also returns file `tris`/`tri_tags`, and GIfTI/STL/FreeSurfer inputs have no tets at all — those are unprotected, and `cullFace(FRONT)` on them is a coin flip.

8. The WebGL2 note is right but names the wrong capability. Verified in Chromium/ANGLE Metal on Apple M2 Max: MAX_DRAW_BUFFERS 8, MAX_COLOR_ATTACHMENTS 8, OES_draw_buffers_indexed present. But WBOIT needs only 2 draw buffers, and 8 is not guaranteed (WebGL2 spec minimum is 4) — so that note is moot. The capability that actually gates WBOIT is a float colour attachment: EXT_color_buffer_half_float + EXT_float_blend (both verified present). §7.1 lists framebuffer formats R8/R16UI/R32F/RGBA8 with no float attachment, so the contract as written cannot host WBOIT at all. Also verified: MAX_SAMPLES 4 and gl_SampleMask absent from plain GLSL ES 3.00 (needs OES_sample_variables, which is present) — so stochastic/alpha-to-coverage transparency is too coarse to be the answer. WEBGL_clip_cull_distance and EXT_clip_control are also present.

9. On WBOIT "washing out": directionally right, but the precise reason is that McGuire-Bavoil's weight is a function of *view-space depth* with curves tuned for alpha in roughly [0.2, 0.9] and game-scale z. A head model spans ~250 mm viewed from ~400 mm; a verbatim implementation will bias badly regardless of contrast.

Confidence 0.85 rather than higher because item 6 means the single most common user action is already adequately handled, so the severity is "major" only for translucent-cortex renders; and one could argue §4 does not literally forbid an engine-internal two-pass.

Replace the finding's per-layer `faceMode:'twoPassSorted'` with a scene-level phase split plus an orientation guarantee. Six concrete contract edits:

  2b. Transparent FRONT faces: `cullFace(BACK)`, depth-test on, depth-write off; objects sorted back-to-front by the depth of their NEAR extent.
